title: FCC on workplace harassment
author: none@none.com (Sara Malkani)
content:
THE commentary that followed the recent Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) judgement dismissing the harassment claim of an NBP employee gives the impression that the court has rolled back the scope of the workplace harassment law so that it now covers only incidents of an ove­r­tly sexual nature, excluding conduct that amounts to gender-based discrimination. This is incorrect.
The correct position of the law now is this: allegations of workplace harassment prior to 2022 (which is when the Protection Against Harassment of Women in the Workplace Act was amended) must involve conduct of an overtly sexual nature to fall within the scope of the law. Actions that take place after the 2022 amendment are covered by the law not only if they are overtly sexual in nature, but also if they are rooted in gender-based discrimination. Let’s see why.
First, let’s look at the definition of ‘harassment’. Prior to January 2022, it was defined to cover “any unwelcome sexual advance, request for sexual favours or other verbal or written communication or physical conduct of a sexual nature or sexually demeaning attitudes, causing interference with work performance or creating an intimidating, hostile, or offensive work environment, or the attempt to punish the complainant for refusal to comply to such a request or is made a condition for employment”.
This definition was amended in January 2022 by adding the following: “discrimination on basis of gender, which may or may not be sexual in nature, but which may embody a discriminatory and prejudicial mindset or notion, resulting in discriminatory behaviour on basis of gender against the complainant” (Section 2[h][ii] of the Act).
The court interpreted the original definition restrictively, following the reasoning of the first Nadia Naz judgement.
The amendment was made after the 2021 Supreme Court decision in Nadia Naz vs President of Pakistan. This case, which analysed and applied the original, pre-2022 definition of harassment, concluded that the law only covers harassment of an overtly sexual nature. The 2022 amendment, passed a few months after the judgement, rectified the limitation in the original definition as interpreted by the Supreme Court in the Nadia Naz judgement of 2021. The amended definition explicitly includes gender-based discrimination within the meaning of harassment.
The amended definition would not apply retrospectively. The expanded definition, which broadens the scope of the actionable wrong, would only cover actions that take place after the amendment.
But in 2023 the Supreme Court, reviewing the Nadia Naz judgement, held that the original definition was broad enough to include gender-based discrimination. Harassment as originally defined should be interpreted to include conduct that is not overtly sexual in nature but amounts to gender-based discrimination. The Supreme Court declared that the bench’s interpretation of the original definition was too restrictive.
The interpretation in the Nadia Naz judgement on review would be brilliant were it not for the 2022 amendment. By interpreting the original definition to have essentially the same meaning and effect as the 2022 insertion, the Supreme Court implies that the 2022 amendment was redundant. This contradicts a basic principle of statutory interpretation, which requires that each statutory provision should be interpreted to give it a distinct meaning.
It may well be that the 2022 amendment was not needed because the original definition should be interpreted as broadly and purposively as the Supreme Court did in the Nadia Naz judgement on review. But when the legislature amended the definition in 2022 to explicitly cover gender-based discrimination, it also implied that the earlier definition was restrictive, which is why the amendment was needed.
By explicitly expanding the de­­finition, it endorsed the view that the original definition did not cover gender-based discrimination.
The FCC in its recent judgement did the same. The FCC interpreted the original definition restrictively, following the reasoning of the first Nadia Naz judgement. It did not refer to the 2022 amendment, and it did not need to because the incidents involved in the case predated the amendment. The amended definition would not apply to these facts. It would have been more edifying if the FCC had clearly explained this, but lucid, well-written judgements are unfortunately uncommon.
Let’s say, as many have argued, that the FCC should have interpreted the original definition more broadly to include gender-based discrimination. What implication would that have for the current definition of harassment? Such an interpretation would entail that the second part of the definition is redundant because the first part covers conduct embodying gender-based discrimination. Such reasoning would again contradict the principle of statutory interpretation, which says that the legislature does not waste its words.
The FCC decision is deeply flawed, but for another reason. The FCC has not applied its own interpretation properly. The harassment at issue in this case was overtly sexual in nature. The evidence put forward at the earlier stages of the case, before the Islamabad High Court and the ombudsperson, shows that the complainant faced harassment that was unambiguously sexual. It is disturbing that the FCC did not consider this conduct to fall within the scope of the original definition.
Flawed as it is, the FCC has not overruled the 2022 amendment to the law. The expanded definition (Section 2(h)(ii)) still stands, but it will only apply to incidents that took place or are alleged to have taken place after the date of the amendment. Prior incidents will be covered by the original definition, which will be interpreted restrictively.
This clarification is important because after the FCC ruling and the outrage against it, many potential claimants believe that the pervasive gender-based discrimination they currently face at the workplace is not covered by the law. People sitting on workplace harassment committees have told me that their mandate is now restricted to only incidents that are overtly sexual in nature. We must remind them that it is not.
The writer is a lawyer and the author of Progressive Laws In Patriarchal Societies.

title: Smaller pie, firmer grip
author: none@none.com (Waqar Wadho)
content:
WHEN railways and factories began transforming 19th-century Europe, the rulers of the Habsburg Empire understood their economic potential. Yet they resisted industrialisation. Friedrich von Gentz, Metternich’s adviser, explained why: “We do not desire at all that the great masses shall become well-off and independent.” His reasoning ended with a revealing question: “How could we otherwise rule over them?” The Habsburg rulers were not necessarily ignorant of the economic benefits of technological progress. They feared its political consequences. A more prosperous society might also become more independent, weakening their grip on power.
This historical episode helps explain a persistent puzzle in Pakistan: why do those in power repeatedly choose institutions (rules of the game) and policies that constrain economic progress, even when they too benefit from better alternatives? The answer may lie in the distinction between economic and political returns. Elites do not necessarily choose arrangements that maximise national income, or even their own immediate economic gains. They also consider how a change might affect their ability to retain power and capture future returns — what we call the political replacement effect in economics.
Technological and institutional changes can expand economic opportunities while simultaneously creating new centres of political power. Incumbents may, therefore, resist changes that threaten their hold on power. The calculation is straightforward. A reform may make the economy larger and even increase the income of existing elites. But if it also raises the probability of their political displacement, or reduces the share of future gains they can command, their expected returns may decline. Under these conditions, elites may rationally prefer an inferior arrangement that preserves their political dominance.
In other words, a smaller pie under a secure scenario may be more attractive than a larger pie with uncertain future distribution.
An economically promising change can redistribute political power.
Pakistan’s recent history offers three institutional and technological choices that are especially revealing. First is local government. The Constitution requires provinces to devolve political, administrative and financial authority to elected local representatives. Yet successive governments have either delayed local elections or weakened the institutions they create. The largest province, Punjab, last held LG elections a decade ago. Other provinces have also adopted various approaches to limit devolution. KP, for example, recently increased the population threshold for village and neighbourhood councils to reduce the number of councils, potentially weakening representation. In Sindh, transfers to LGs declined from 15.7 per cent of provincial general revenue receipts to just 5.8pc in the 2025-26 budget.
What makes these choices economically questionable? Elected LGs with genuine fiscal and administrative authority can better respond to local needs, improve service delivery, and strengthen accountability. Why, then, resist them? Because empowered LGs also create political competitors. A mayor controlling development funds and public services can build an independent political constituency. Legislators lose influence over resources that help sustain their electoral networks. Even if improved local governance generates greater prosperity, its political dividends may accrue to someone else.
The second example is fiscal federalism. The seventh NFC award raised provinces’ share of the divisible pool to 57.5pc, with constitutional protection against subsequent reductions. But since then, the federal government has built a parallel fiscal system undermining the very principle of federalism. Petroleum levy collections, which are not shared with provinces, reached Rs1.567 trillion in 2025-26. Provinces were also asked to generate surpluses and, lately, to provide grants to the federal government.
The parallel system may be responding to genuine fiscal pressures, but it preserves fiscal discretion at the centre, despite the constitutional commitment to provincial autonomy. In essence, after the seventh NFC, the provincial share fell without anyone touching the award. The political economy consideration here is that meaningful fiscal autonomy changes the distribution of power. Provinces with independent revenue sources and predictable resources can pursue their own priorities and strengthen their political standing.
But the provinces are no different. While demanding autonomy from Islamabad, they resist transferring meaningful authority and resources to elected LGs. At each tier, those holding resources resist passing them down.
The third example concerns technology: rooftop solar. Faced with high electricity tariffs, the public began investing in their own power generation. Solar offered consumers cheaper electricity, greater reliability, and reduced dependence on the national grid. Yet policy increasingly moved towards discouraging its adoption. The government not only imposed a 10pc sales tax on solar panels but, in February, it replaced net metering with net billing for new connections, substantially lowering the compensation for surplus electricity supplied to the grid. A more economically sustainable response would have restructured costly contractual obligations, modernised the grid, and established fair charges for network use.
Why has such adjustment proved so difficult? One explanation is that decentralised electricity generation threatens more than power producers’ revenues. It also weakens an established system through which economic resources, contracts, subsidies, and regulatory discretion are concentrated. These instruments carry financial and political value. Reforming them could improve overall economic performance while reducing the influence of those who currently control them.
These three cases are not identical, but they share a key feature: an economically promising change can redistribute political power, creating incentives for incumbents to resist or dilute it. This is what makes the political replacement argument more powerful than the familiar explanation that elites protect their economic rents. Sometimes they may sacrifice economic gains, including their own, to preserve the political position from which future gains can be secured.
The implication is that Pakistan’s development problem cannot be resolved through better policy advice alone. The harder challenge is creating institutions that reduce the ability of those in power to obstruct changes that might eventually displace them. The stakes extend beyond the current examples. AI is creating new opportunities while challenging existing economic and political hierarchies. Whether or not Pakistan embraces those opportunities will depend largely on how it responds to a technology most capable of redistributing power.
Until the existing calculations change, the country may continue choosing a smaller pie for the sake of a firmer grip.
The writer is an associate professor of economics at the Lahore School of Economics.

title: Cashless ambition
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE prime minister’s call for a time-bound roadmap to make all payments digital has given the government’s cashless economy drive a target. Federal and provincial institutions are moving towards digital payments, with most expected to complete the transition by December. Raast QR codes are being promoted for transactions, while cheque-based payments through Asaan Assignment Accounts are to be replaced by electronic transfers from Nov 15. These steps could make public transactions easier to trace and reduce delays. But the proposed target of 100pc digital payments raises a question: can the state guarantee reliable access to a system on which it wants everyone to depend?
The PM has rightly linked the plan to nationwide internet access. In many areas, however, patchy mobile signals, power outages and the cost of smartphones and data remain obstacles. A payment method that works smoothly in a major city may be unusable in a remote village. The government says it is developing arrangements for areas without internet connectivity, but these must be tested before cash options are withdrawn. The shift also requires help for small traders, older citizens and people unfamiliar with banking applications. Simply displaying a QR code will not resolve failed transactions, mistaken transfers, or the difficulty of obtaining assistance. There is also the question of trust. Digital payment systems must protect users from fraud, safeguard personal information, and offer procedures for complaints and refunds. Public agencies should publish measurable progress, including transaction failure rates and access in underserved districts, rather than celebrating the number of accounts or QR codes created. Digitising welfare payments deserves particular scrutiny: beneficiaries must be able to receive and use their money without paying intermediaries or travelling long distances. The government should make digital transactions the easiest choice through dependable services and modest costs, not turn them into an obligation before the country is ready. A deadline is useful only if it measures public access.

title: Midterm surprise
author: none@none.com (Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry)
content:
THAT the Republican Party would lose the midterm elections for the US Congress was never in doubt. It was its overwhelming defeat that surprised everyone. Demo­crats have attained a clear majority in the 100-member US Senate (54 Demo­crats, 44 Republicans) and a massive lead in the 435-member House of Represen­tatives (253 Democrats, 157 Republicans). What explains this major shift? One plausible answer is the Iran war and its effects on gas prices, inflation, and the higher cost of living. Importantly, America’s younger population never owned this war. It has been widely seen as Israel’s war that America was fighting. Vice President J.D. Vance has rightly concluded that “the reason we lost [in the elections] is the war”. Even Donald Trump acknowledged that the war with Iran was a factor, though he defended its objectives.
While the Iran war and its side effects may have been the main reason for the Republicans’ defeat, several other factors also weighed in. In his election campaigns, Trump had opposed distant wars, yet he entered into one with Iran at the behest of Israel. American voters saw this as a clear repudiation of the ‘America First’ approach that Trump had touted in his speeches. It was hard for Americans to accept America’s subordination to Israeli interests. This, in turn, raised questions about US legislators’ links with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, whose activities are aligned closely with the agenda of a foreign government (Israel), Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and US complicity by continuing to provide weapons and assistance to Israel. All this did not sit well with young Americans.
How will it impact America’s foreign policy? Two aspects merit attention. First, Trump is unlikely to resume the war with Iran or follow through on his threats to use the mother of all bombs against Iran. The reason is clear. His Republican Party will not want a return to a war that is so unpopular with Americans. A return to war could jeopardise the party’s future stakes, including the race for the White House. In fact, America would like to see an honourable exit from the war. The answer lies in diplomacy and a return to the Islamabad MoU, which meets both the key US demand that Iran should not produce nuclear weapons and the Iranian demand that economic sanctions be lifted and Iran’s frozen assets released. This provides an honourable off-ramp to both sides to end a war that serves no one but Israel.
As for the Strait of Hormuz, everyone wants it to reopen fully because disrupted supplies of oil, gas, petroleum products, and fertilisers have been hurting the world economy. To that end, America should end its naval blockade, and Iran should agree not to interrupt shipping in the strait. All these points have been amply covered in the Islamabad MoU. The parties to the Makkah Agreement — Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye — have a special role. They must increase their diplomatic efforts, as should Qatar and Oman. Even China and Russia may need to step in to help find a diplomatic solution. China, in particular, has an interest in ensuring fuel supplies and the smooth functioning of markets. The window of opportunity may be limited, as the caretaker Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, might plan some manoeuvre, a false flag operation, or some drastic action like using a tactical nuclear weapon to force Iran to respond and then rope the US into the war with Iran.
Republicans will not want to return to a war unpopular with Americans.
The second aspect of US foreign policy relevant to us is whether it will affect Pakistan-US ties. The latter have always been transactional and viewed through America’s own geopolitical interests. As of now, post-Ma­rka-i-Haq Pakistan continues to enjoy respect as a stabilising force in the region. Further, gi­­ven that Afgha­nis­tan is once again becoming a safe haven for the wor­ld’s terrorist organisations, Pakistan’s geopolitical importance as the only state fighting terrorism in all its forms, including proxy terrorism by India from Afghanistan, will remain valid. Pakistan has flourishing bilateral trade with the US, along with cooperation in multiple areas, including agriculture and IT. Relations between Pakistan and the US are, thus, likely to continue at their own pace.
Although many in the ranks of the De­­mocrats tend to have pro-Israel, pro-India, anti-Iran, and anti-China sentiments — si­­m­­­ilar to the Republicans — American foreign policy will remain a major subject of discussion in the Democrats-dominated Con­­­gress in the months ahead. Trans­at­la­n­tic allian­ces, relations with Canada, adventures like Venezuela, opposition to climate change, tariff wars, Islamophobia, subservience to Israeli interests, and Trump’s refusal to regulate AI technologies could all be up for review when the re-composed Congress starts its work next January.
The writer is a former foreign secretary of Pakistan.
Published in Dawn, November 8th, 2026

title: Exchange rate’s woeful tale
author: none@none.com (Ishrat Husain)
content:
THE preoccupation of exchange rate fundamentalists in Pakistan with a single, partial indicator — Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) — is astonishing. As Nadeem ul Haque argued in an illuminating article, fixing or deliberately boosting exchange rates effectively ended with Bretton Woods’ collapse in the 1970s. Research has since confirmed that the exchange rate is a market price — the price of one currency in terms of another, determined by underlying economic conditions — and not a policy tool. Hence, the exchange rate is an endogenous variable reflecting domestic inflation, productivity, external balances, capital flows, reserve adequacy, fiscal credibility, interest-rate differentials, and market expectations. As Haque notes, “The rupee does not weaken because someone decides to weaken it. It weakens because underlying conditions make the existing price unsustainable.”
REER has a legitimate but limited purpose. It measures changes in the nominal exchange rate adjusted for relative price movements against trading partners. But an index reading of 100, based on a selected base year, doesn’t establish an optimal exchange rate. Nor does a deviation from 100 automatically signal overvaluation or undervaluation. REER says little about balance-of-payments sustainability, foreign exchange availability from non-trade sources or exporters’ ability to compete through quality, technology, productivity, and delivery. There are questions to address before treating REER as an authoritative guide to exchange rate policy.
First, does the base year 2010 represent an equilibrium exchange rate? Pakistan recorded a current account deficit of $3.95 billion, around two per cent of GDP, that year, compared with a near-balanced account in 2026. Second, have trade weights and trading partner composition remained representative over 16 years, especially after the China FTA? Third, have movements in individual partners’ currencies been adequately reflected in an index referencing the US dollar? Fourth, the choice of price deflator (CPI, PPI, unit labour costs or GDP deflator) can produce very different results. These points need serious thought before prescriptions are based on a single index.
REER doesn’t capture many of the external account components. Workers’ remittances have grown faster than merchandise exports. They’re a major source of foreign exchange, financing imports of raw material, equipment and fuel, enabling domestic industry to use productive capacity that would otherwise be underemployed. They help build reserves, boost external stability, and reduce reliance on borrowing. FDI, portfolio investment, and external debt disbursements provide more foreign exchange liquidity. Assessments limited to REER overlook these determinants of external sustainability.
Questions must be addressed before treating REER as an authoritative guide to exchange rate policy.
Three empirical tests help establish whether the exchange rate is artificially managed or broadly market-determined. The first is the differential between official interbank and open-market rates. It peaked at Rs10-15 per dollar in FY2023. As reserves accumulated and market conditions normalised, the gap narrowed to its customary Rs0.50-2 range, indicating a more unified foreign exchange market. The second test is whether administrative restrictions on imports and profit and dividend repatriation are being used to suppress foreign exchange demand. Such curbs were imposed in FY2023 when SBP reserves fell to $3bn or so. Imports declined to $53bn and profit and dividend repatriation to just $331 million against normal levels of about $70bn and $2bn. Last fiscal, imports recovered to $71bn. Profit and dividend remittances reached $2.3bn. Arrears were cleared and current obligations met. This restoration hardly supports the view that the exchange rate is being sustained through administrative demand suppression. The third, perhaps most compelling, test is whether SBP has depleted its reserves to defend a parity. In FY2023, reserves fell to about $3bn recovering to around $21bn despite annual external debt-servicing dues of about $25bn. This accumulation occurred while the rate was around Rs280 per dollar and REER above 100. It’s difficult to reconcile this outcome with the claim that an artificial exchange rate is being maintained when SBP is mopping up surplus dollar liquidity after interbank clearance.
Historical comparisons reinforce this view. Bet­ween 2015 and 2018, the rupee was maintained aro­­und Rs104 per dollar, but SBP reserves dec­li­ned from $18bn to $9bn. In contrast, in 2000-2007 when reserves increased from barely $1bn to $13bn, the exchange rate remained stable around Rs60 and exports more than doubled from $9bn to $19bn. Still, critics said the rate was artificially defended, overlooking the net foreign exchange inflows being sterilised to prevent excessive appreciation and protect exporters’ competitiveness.
Market expectations are another important aspect. In Pakistan, they are often driven by a bandwagon effect instead of rational assessments of fundamentals. When reserves fall below comfortable levels, depreciation expectations can become self-fulfilling. Exporters withhold dollar proceeds within the permitted 90-day surrender period, anticipating a better rate; importers advance foreign exchange requirements to avoid future depreciation. Supply contracts and demand rises putting pressure on the rupee. The anticipated depreciation then materialises.
Would a 10pc depreciation advocated by REER fundamentalists improve competitiveness? Foreign buyers may demand price discounts of at least 5pc from exporters, treating additional rupee earnings as a windfall. About 40pc of exports use imported inputs including fuel, LNG, and textile raw materials. Their costs rise, leaving exporters with a net gain of perhaps only 2-3pc. The impact goes beyond exporters. Costlier imports fuel inflation, hurting poorer households whose main asset is their labour and whose wages, particularly in an informal economy with extensive underemployment, do not adjust proportionately. The central bank may raise interest rates, increasing domestic borrowing costs. Imported machinery becomes costlier, forcing investors to put off or abandon projects, hurting both investment and growth. As the rupee cost of servicing external debt increases, partly offset by higher import-duty collections, government may have to borrow more, crowding out private-sector credit. Foreign investors earn lower dollar returns, discouraging fresh investment.
The lesson is that exchange-rate stability can’t be engineered through administrative intervention or depreciation alone. It must rest on credible fiscal management, a broader tax base, sound trade and tariff policies, remunerative energy pricing, higher productivity and prudent monetary management. Together, these policies reduce the need for disruptive exchange-rate adjustments.
Pakistan must not treat REER as a magic number and depreciation as a remedy. The aim should not be an arbitrary index reading but sustainable external competitiveness, stronger reserves, higher exports and investment, and protection of purchasing power. The exchange rate is a reflection of economic fundamentals, not a substitute for them. Correcting symptoms while neglecting underlying weaknesses will only perpetuate the rupee’s woeful tale. 
The writer is a former State Bank governor.
Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026

title: When home is hell
author: none@none.com (E.N. Bandial)
content:
ON an ordinary March afternoon this year, the children of a household in Lahore’s Choong district gathered for their uncle’s small promise of treats. Among them was four-year-old Azan, who was led out for a stroll by his uncle. It all ended eight hours later in the isolated outskirts of Quaid-i-Azam Industrial Estate — with Azan dead. The minor’s body, when recovered, showed a two-inch exposed spinal cord attaching the head and mutilated remains. Azan had reportedly been tortured and eventually killed with an eight-inch-long knife by his own father, allegedly in a calculated bid to implicate a third party. Azan is just one of several children who are killed every month by people known to them.
Moving back, in October, a 13-year-old in Mianwali was shot dead by her cousin for not wearing a hijab. In September, a three-year-old in Islamabad was kidnapped, raped, and murdered by her brother-in-law. In August, an 18-month-old in Karachi died after being raped by her 17-year-old cousin, while in July, a six-year-old boy was beaten up, raped, and strangled with a wire by his neighbour, and a four-year-old girl in Gujranwala was set on fire by her mother on suspicion of being ‘possessed’. In May, a father in Vehari repeatedly raped his three daughters aged 14, 11, and nine for six consecutive months; while three children aged six, four, and three were killed and found hanging from the fans in their home in Multan. A month earlier, in April, a mother in Lahore brutally slit the throats of her three children, luring them through a sadistic ‘game’ of hide-and-seek.
Occurring within the safe confines of the home, these tragedies shocked and enraged us more than others, but our protest ended in quiet resignation, as it did in 2022 when an eight-year-old was tortured and poisoned by her grandparents for failing at household chores, and in 2015 when a 12-year-old was beaten to death by her father for not making properly round rotis. 
Homes repeatedly turn into hell for children as our criminal justice system is unequipped to intercept and prevent attacks within the home. Statutes such as the ICT and Sindh Child Protection Acts create institutional bodies that address minors’ welfare, but they lack the authority to adopt anticipatory, prompt, and intrusive measures to ensure child safety. Our laws are reactive rather than anticipatory. Even the landmark Zainab Alert, Response, and Recovery Act, 2020, creates a protection mechanism for missing children that is enforceable only after the abduction is reported. As a result, attacks on children in public are not easily prevented.
Our criminal justice system is unequipped to intercept and prevent attacks within the home.
Recently, a five-year-old in Haripur was raped and left to die after being lured out of her home to see her father; an eight-year-old in Lahore was sexually harassed in a grocery store by the owner, and an eight-year-old in Sargodha was raped and murdered in a grocery store. Even when these victims were seen being accompanied or coaxed by a group of men or being eyed by strangers, the palpable threat of attack was ignored by those present at the scene. It was also in the presence of bystanders in Multan that 15-year-old Wasim was tortured and then run over by his employer recently. Whether it was their indifference or ignorance, they abandoned the weakest, most vulnerable members of society — our children. Being voiceless, defenceless and weak, children are considered dispensable. It is, therefore, easy to ignore injustices against them.
We tolerate inadequate child protection laws and mechanisms, ignore the proliferation of pornographic content, disregard paedophilic customs such as trading minor boys, and permit appalling lectures advocating marriage with girls as young as four. Our complicity and apathy have normalised child abuse and allowed it to persist, putting Pakistan third on the global map for child abuse. Around 2,000 cases of child abuse were reported in just the first six months of the current year. Sahil reported over 3,600 in 2025. In 2024, 21 children were being abused daily. Reducing such horrifying figures demands enforceable protection under the law. Justice Jawad Hasan in 2023 (Zafar Khizer vs the Federation of Pakistan)initiated a shift in discourse from viewing children as ordinary citizens to viewing them as vulnerable citizens categorised as ‘child citizens’ and entitled to a higher degree of protection and concern under the law. Justice Usman G. Rashid last month said that the child citizen is entitled to fundamental rights in their independent capacity that cannot be displaced by any parental authority. While the concept of the child citizen as an independent rights holder is evolving through jurisprudence, it is insufficient without effective implementation and accountability.
Mandatory reporting regimes should be introduced for designated professionals such as healthcare providers, instructors, and adults in child-related roles or positions of trust, as under Australian law and England’s Crime and Policing Act, 2026. Additional measures for prevention through reporting suspected child abuse and conducting child-sensitive investigations and follow-ups in such cases must be made compulsory in line with the spirit of Article 19 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. These obligations must be rooted not merely in law, but in a shared sense of humanity and a collective duty to protect the vulnerable because, as lawyer and human rights activist Asma Jahangir said, a society that fails to protect its children has, in fact, failed humanity’s most basic test. 
The writer is a lawyer.
Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026

Pakistan's criminal justice system and existing child protection statutes (e.g., ICT and Sindh Child Protection Acts, Zainab Alert Act) are reactive and ill-equipped to intercept or prevent domestic child abuse proactively.
Societal complicity, apathy, and the normalization of practices like child marriage, coupled with inadequate laws, contribute significantly to Pakistan ranking third globally in child abuse cases.

Recent judicial jurisprudence is evolving to recognize children as 'child citizens' with independent fundamental rights, but effective implementation and accountability remain a significant challenge.

The article advocates for mandatory reporting regimes by designated professionals, child-sensitive investigations, and measures rooted in collective humanity, referencing international standards like Article 19 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

title: The debt burden
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S external debt has nearly doubled in a decade — from $68.7bn in 2015 to $135.1bn in 2025 — according to a new World Bank report. Public and publicly guaranteed debt accounts for $107.1bn of the total, private debt for $17.6bn, and short-term borrowing for $10.45bn.
China is the largest single creditor with $22.4bn outstanding, followed by the World Bank and Asian Development Bank. The rise itself is not surprising but the pace is striking. Much of this borrowing went towards plugging external financing gaps, propping up reserves, and repaying older loans to keep the economy running.
    
The debt spike describes an economy that invests, produces and earns too little to service what it owes. Debt has become the main constraint on our fiscal and economic prospects. Servicing debt eats up meagre financial resources, which should be expanding productive capacity for exports, and makes faster growth harder to reach. That leads to more borrowing.
The government borrows to cover consumption, budget deficits, and external payments — not to build anything that pays for itself. Development spending is usually the first thing to be cut, and growth has crawled along at 2.7pc in recent years.
There is nothing wrong with borrowing. Developing economies need foreign capital for infrastructure, energy, technology, and industry. The trouble starts when loans do not raise domestic productivity or lift exports. Successive governments have failed to tell apart borrowing that builds capacity from borrowing that only buys time. Pakistan’s recurring balance-of-payments crisis underscores this fact.
    
The country’s exports are weak, the production base is narrow, investment is low, and fiscal deficits refuse to go away. So, the economy keeps relying on foreign and domestic loans. Remittances, rollovers by friendly countries, and one IMF programme after another may have staved off immediate default, but none of them has addressed the underlying problem.
It does not matter much if the country can raise another loan or defer another repayment. What matters is whether the country can generate enough growth, tax revenue, and foreign exchange to meet its obligations without sacrificing its development.
The situation calls for a credible, short- to long-term strategy to invest in projects that raise productivity, exports, and foreign exchange earnings. The strategy must be accompanied by wider reforms aimed at expansion of the tax base, more productive public spending, and lower costs of doing business.
Exporters need energy that is reliable and competitively priced, policies they can predict, and access to modern technology. Without these, even fresh foreign investment and cheaper credit will yield little value, growth will remain anaemic, children stunted, and communities without basic services such as clean drinking water. And debt will continue to constrain the country’s economic sovereignty and prosperity.
Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026

title: Expendable LGs
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
POLITICAL parties frequently appear reluctant to hold regular local bodies elections on one pretext or another. This attitude negates constitutional requirements for holding local government polls and establishing LGs, denying voters the right to elect their representatives at the grassroots level. As reported, the ECP has dropped plans to hold LG polls in KP due to the suspension of Article 140-A. After the proclamation of emergency in the province last month, the article had been suspended in specific districts. The centre has now suspended Article 140-A across the province, scuttling plans for LG polls in the foreseeable future. Questions have also been raised regarding the LG polls scheduled in Islamabad for Dec 20, as a petitioner has challenged delimitation in the high court. In Punjab, however, LG polls should be held in February 2027, unless new obstructions are created.
It is unfortunate that both the state and political parties — which claim to be the flag-bearers of democracy — put in so much effort to keep third-tier governance in indefinite abeyance. Under the law, elections are supposed to take place 120 days after the term of an LG expires. However, in Pakistan, the law is routinely flouted. In KP, the LGs’ term expired in June, while in Punjab and Islamabad Capital Territory, LG polls should have been held in May 2022 and June 2021, respectively. A common tactic, particularly used by parties ruling a province, is to amend the LG laws so that delimitation and the electoral process are further postponed. This ploy ends up wasting taxpayers’ money and depriving citizens of their right to elect local representatives. To do away with the legal loopholes, it has been suggested that the Elections Act, 2017, be amended so that no changes to the LG law are allowed once an LG completes its term. Secondly, a constitutional amendment may be required to clarify the process of LG polls so that neither the centre nor the provinces can shirk this essential responsibility. Our cities, towns, and villages cannot develop without functioning and responsive LGs. Moreover, empowered local bodies also present a democratic alternative to the complicated question of forging new provinces, as they would, in theory, bring power and funds down to the local level.
Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026
topic: Local Government System, Democratic Decentralization, and Constitutional Compliance in Pakistan

Aspirants can use its arguments to demonstrate an understanding of governance challenges, constitutional breaches, and potential reforms in essays on democracy, federalism, and public administration.

The suspension of Article 140-A in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and challenges to delimitation in Islamabad exemplify the systemic pretexts used to indefinitely postpone LG polls.
A common tactic involves amending local government laws after an LG's term expires, leading to delays, wasted taxpayer money, and disenfranchisement.

Suggested reforms include amending the Elections Act, 2017 to prevent post-expiry law changes, and a constitutional amendment to clarify the LG poll processes, ensuring accountability and promoting local development.

title: Enabling terrorism
author: none@none.com (Dr Raashid Wali Janjua)
content:
INSURGENCIES militarise society and spawn a conflict economy that empowers splinter insurgent groups with their own set of interests and objectives. These militant groups thrive in a governance vacuum as well as the ideological confusion in post-conflict societies. The TTP is amongst the classic examples of insurgency-begotten militancy and terrorism. Afghanistan is a quintessential case study of an insurgency-wracked nation that has given rise to other insurgencies and waves of terrorism.
Afghanistan’s 10-year anti-Soviet insurgency achieved success but spawned another decade of internecine conflict that gave space to terrorist entities and subsequent international intervention against Al Qaeda terrorists operating from that country. Pakistan’s action against terrorist entities elicited an irate response from these violent groups in the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (now merged districts of KP), leading to a series of military operations from 2004 to 2017, driving the terrorists towards Afghanistan.
After the US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021, the Taliban regime occupied Kabul and reneged on all its pledges made in the Doha Agreement and introduced a brutal, oppressive regime where there was no place for minorities, women, and non-Taliban Afghans. Soon after assuming power, the Taliban regime gave free rein to terrorist entities like the TTP and freed hardened criminals and terrorists from jails.
After the US withdrawal, Pakistan extended an olive branch to the Taliban regime, offering humanitarian aid, trade facilities, and economic integration. But despite continual positive engagement, the Taliban did not abide by their counterterrorism commitments. Terrorist entities like TTP were given free rein to operate against Pakistan from secure sanctuaries in Afghanistan. When Pakistan started tightening its noose against these terrorists, their leadership was reportedly taken to Kabul’s Green Zone and hid amongst the civilian population.
Insurgencies in Afghanistan have created an ecosystem of terror.
At present, a blend of over 20 terrorist entities is operating under the benign gaze of the Taliban regime in Afghanistan. The Taliban are extremely adept at denialism and selling their anti-IS-K credentials. The reality is different, however, as terrorist entities like IS-K with a transnational agenda are operating under an entente cordiale between them and the Taliban regime. For many foreign powers, the Doha Agreement has been reduced to just two points — women’s rights and education — relegating inclusivity to the backburner due to the international community’s predilection for appeasing the Taliban.
Pakistan is paying a huge price for this indulgence of the Taliban. After the US withdrawal, terrorist attacks in Pakistan surged manifold. Thousands have been killed and injured in terrorist attacks since. The two-faced Taliban have perfected the art of denying complicity in terrorism to curry favour with foreign donors. They are being facilitated in this endeavour by hostile foreign intelligence agencies that wish to keep the region destabilised for their geopolitical interests.
The Taliban regime is thriving on an illicit economy where narco-trafficking, smuggling and extortion are being sponsored under official patronage, with the Taliban warlords having stakes in each criminal enterprise.
The weapons left by Nato and US forces are being sold to terrorist entities. American and Nato forces, after the 2021 withdrawal, left behind weapons and equipment worth $7.12 billion, out of which large quantities were handed over or sold to terrorist entities like the TTP by the Taliban. Terrorist groups including the TTP and BLA have used these weapons against Pakistan under the patronage of the Taliban re­­­-gi­­me.
According to the April 2025 report of the US Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction, the TTP accessed former Afghan army weapons, either transferred by Taliban authorities or acquired through the black market. Similar confirmation has been made by the UN Security Council Monitoring Team.
By 2025, Pakistan’s security forces had recovered 293 US-made weapons and other gear from eliminated terrorists. Even a 2025 Washington Post investigation traced serial numbers of at least 63 weapons seized in Pakistan from terrorists to weapons supplied by the US to Afghan forces before 2021.
Earlier insurgencies in Afghanistan birthed an ecosystem of terror, which is now being exported. The flow of arms to terrorist entities like the TTP and BLA from Afghanistan under the patronage of the Afghan Taliban regime is a taste of things to come for the entire international community, whose attention at present is consumed mostly by the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. 
The writer is a security analyst with a PhD degree from NUST.

title: American change
author: none@none.com (Rafia Zakaria)
content:
ON the Sunday before Election Day in the US, the Democratic leadership was in uproar. The reason was Israel — though not obviously so. The action took place in Detroit, Michigan, where Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed was in a close race against Republican Mike Rogers. Rogers had run a campaign marked by Islamo­phobic attacks on El-Sayed’s Muslim faith, portraying him as a security threat and making unfounded allegations of extremist sympathies.
In the primary election that decided the Democratic nominee, El-Sayed had defeated Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who had said she “dreamed of Israel” and had benefited from nearly $30 million in spending by pro-Israel lobbies. Despite this, El-Sayed was able to win.
Stevens decided that Sunday morning that she would endorse El-Sayed’s opponent, a man she had previously criticised. It was an extraordinary move that drew condemnation from her fellow Democrats and the American left. Appearing at an African-American church alongside Rogers, Stevens said that she just couldn’t support El-Sayed and would, instead, back the Republican.
    
For the 48 hours until the election, Stevens got tons of attention. In an interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper, she struggled to explain why she had withdrawn support for a candidate she had previously endorsed. Pro-Zionist commentators on the American right were gleeful.
Maybe they hoped El-Sayed, who had openly opposed the war against Iran and called Gaza a genocide, would not win. It was a close election, and Stevens might persuade some Black and Jewish voters in Michigan not to vote for the man who would become the first Muslim senator in US history.
As we know now, their predictions were wrong. El-Sayed defeated Rogers, becoming the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Democrats also won control of both Houses of Congress, while several Muslim candidates, including Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib and Andre Carson won election or re-election.
Democrat victories show voters oppose blanket support for Israel.
Of all of them, El-Sayed had been the most plainspoken about the problem with US support for Israel. The particular mastery of his campaign was that it took the very Trumpian rhetoric of ‘America First’ and turned it on its head. El-Sayed argued that politicians who prioritised billions in aid to Israel over domestic needs were putting another country’s interests before those of ordinary Americans.
This message resonated with voters all around the country. The issue of whether a politician is ‘America First’ rather than ‘Israel First’ has become part of the political conversation. This is particularly worrisome for establishment Democrats who would compete to demonstrate their love for Israel.
    
The Democratic victories have clearly shown that the party voter wants to end the blanket support for Israel that has long been an American tradition. Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, presumptive leaders of the Senate and House, have both said that they do not support sending unending aid to Israel. They know which way the wind is blowing.
The biggest evidence of this, however, came from the Republicans — really from the vice president himself. Even as the results were coming in, J.D. Vance took to X and wrote a lengthy post on why his party had lost so abysmally. Vance pointed directly to the war in Iran — which America entered at Israel’s behest — saying it had cost Republicans the election. It was a shocking yet understandable acknowledgment. It made sense for Vance — who is likely to run for president in 2028 — to try and distance himself from Trump right away. Now, he is seeking to ally himself with anti-Israel figures on the American right like Tucker Carlson.
Car­lson’s opposition to Israel is pointed in that he said he wou­ld have voted for El-Sayed simply be­­cause he was so fed up with unending support for Israel, which he thought had a harmful influence on America’s politics. Carlson has urged his supporters to understand how American democracy was being turned into a sham by Israeli influence.
    
The America that woke up on Nov 4, 2026, is, therefore, a remarkably different America. Israel’s government has long relied on strong bipartisan support in Washington, and pro-Israel organisations have spent enormous sums to ensure that American politicians will always be in their pocket. Those days are not decisively over.
It is likely that when the new lawmakers take office in January, legislation and limits will be pursued on all aid to Israel that could see the amount of military support drastically reduced. America voted for change this week but it is likely that it is Israel — with much reduced US support after January — that will see the greatest change in its circumstances.
The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.

title: Human bondage
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
BONDED labour is modern-day slavery. It exists in Pakistan as a system of generational exploitation sustained by abject poverty, debt, and feudal power.
The recent praise for Pakistan from the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights for raising the minimum marriageable age to 18 is, no doubt, welcome. It follows the committee’s review of Pakistan’s second periodic report. But questions about the high numbers of child brides and bonded labour eclipse the compliment. Underage marriage is enslavement, while the purchase of bricks produced through debt bondage by construction companies and government groups continues to sustain the curse of bonded labour. Lifespans rarely outlast the loans driven up by interest charges. Generations inherit a cycle of debt and abuse.
    
The scourge does not spare children, who begin life in inhuman working and living conditions. Entire families slog for pathetic sums far below the legal minimum wage. The Constitution outlaws all forced labour and slavery; the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1992, criminalises the practice.
Yet, the failure to enforce the law and insufficient efforts to bridge the distance between constitutional rights and their fulfilment have forced poor people into a life of bondage. Punjab has over 210,000 documented kiln workers while more than 2,900 victims of forced labour were recorded last year.
According to The State of Peasant Rights in Sindh, 2025, 1,311 labourers in the province were rescued from brick kilns and the farm sector. Patterns of enforcement are reactive and often set off by media attention or judicial intervention. Injustices — verbal abuse, beating, murder, and torture — prevail because spot inspections are absent. As per the National Commission for Human Rights, women routinely experience sexual abuse and forced marriages. Law enforcement and political quarters are notorious for protecting the perpetrators, instead of ensuring legal implementation. Systemic coercion will keep Pakistan from becoming a humane state.
Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

The exploitation extends to entire families, including children, who are forced to work under inhuman conditions for wages far below the legal minimum, enduring severe physical and sexual abuse.
Enforcement efforts are primarily reactive, triggered by media attention or judicial intervention, highlighting a broader failure of state institutions and political will to uphold human rights.

title: Rule of the people?
author: none@none.com (Aasim Sajjad Akhtar)
content:
THE resounding defeat of the Republican Party in the US midterm election this week has triggered celebratory chatter around the world. Many see it as the beginning of the end for Donald Trump; the vibe was very similar when Trump was defeated by Joe Biden in the 2020 US presidential election. Yet four years later, Trumpism proved to be alive and very well.
Trump cannot stand in the 2028 presidential election. For that reason alone, his political career is reaching its end. But that does not mean that Trumpism — both the ideology and the social base to which it speaks — will disappear alongside the man himself.
Here I offer some suggestions what this latest election signals about the future of democracy in the US, and, by extension, around the world.
We should harbour no illusions about the power of big money in American politics, or the Democratic Party’s historical commitment to US empire — the Biden administration’s diabolical warmongering after Oct 7, 2023, in Gaza, after all, set the stage for Trump’s 2024 win. Given this backdrop, the victory of candidates like Abdul el-Sayed who oppose imperialist wars abroad and are fronting progressive economic policies at home — just like Zohran Mamdani did during his successful campaign to become New York mayor — confirms that societal attitudes are changing. A growing number of young Americans now view socialism favourably and want unconditional support for Israel to be discontinued. It is another matter entirely whether an increasingly influential left-wing of the Democratic Party can win the inner-party struggle and then the presidency.
The contemporary state is whittling away democratic freedoms.
While progressive ideology has gained a foothold in American society, the Trumpist right maintains its powerful, and mobilised MAGA base, sustained in part by Christian evangelicals. Before his win in 2024, Trump vowed to stop fighting wars abroad, and bring back industrial jobs and prosperity. His base has been antagonised by the disastrous and prolonged war on Iran, and the inflationary spiral it has triggered. Vice-President J.D. Vance has already acknowledged this, and even added that Washington’s ‘special relationship’ with Israel must change. Trumpism will not die out because of a midterm defeat. Long-term economic stagnation will give it social mooring, while its major ideological enemies — immigration, the left, and outsourcing — remain easy sells.
A useful analogy is that of Brazil, where Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva recently staved off the most recent articulation of Bolsanarismo — the parallel ideology to Trumpism — to win his fourth term as president. Brazil’s left has far greater social roots than the emergent Democratic left in the US, hence its ability to mobilise the last-minute votes necessary to re-elect Lula. But the far right under the leadership of the Bolsanaro family also has a mobilised social base, which will rebound from the election loss. Lula is 81, and his Workers Party will have to deepen the social struggle to keep Bolsanarismo at bay in the years to come.
Zooming out further, the right wing is ascendant across much of the world, while the contemporary state is whittling away democratic freedoms and paving the way for capital to carry on with business as usual. Electoral victories for left-of-centre candidates in the US, Brazil or wherever else they may come to pass will not produce structural change in isolation. Does going to the ballot allow ordinary people an opportunity to exercise political choice? Yes. But this is not the same as working-class majorities being organised for progressive social transformation. The latter is re­­quired both to ensure more significant electo­r­­al success and then to turn such victories into su­­bstantive cha­­­nge.
Of course, we in Pakistan do not even get to enjoy the unfettered right to vote. The military-bureaucratic oligarchy that has ruled over us from soon after 1947 did not even allow a general election until 1970, and then chose military action rather than handing over power to the winning party afterwards. More recently, the electoral mandate in the 2024 general election was stolen blatantly, culminating in the imposition of emergency in KP. There is something to be said for at least the temporary waves of hope that are generated by electoral victories, even if one should at the same time be conscious of the highly delimited nature of democracy under the rule of contemporary capital. Progressives in Pakistan have to fight an epic battle against tyranny to even retain the pretence that democracy means rule of the people. And then we have to come up with a shared project for how to run a country ravaged by violence, repression and a deep crisis of identity.
The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.
Published in Dawn, November 6th, 2026

whyMatters: This article offers a critical analysis of the global state of democracy, using the US and Brazil as case studies to illustrate the resilience of right-wing populism (Trumpism, Bolsonarismo) even after electoral defeats. It highlights the challenges faced by progressive movements and the crucial distinction between electoral victories and substantive structural change, making it vital for understanding contemporary political dynamics.

Despite a global ascendance of the right, a progressive left is gaining influence in the US, challenging imperialist policies and advocating for progressive economic reforms, though its capacity for structural change remains uncertain.

The article argues that the contemporary state is globally whittling away democratic freedoms, paving the way for capital, and that electoral victories alone are insufficient for achieving fundamental societal transformation without organized working-class majorities.

In countries like Pakistan, even the unfettered right to vote is suppressed by a military-bureaucratic oligarchy, presenting an 'epic battle' for progressives to retain the pretense of democracy and address deep national crises.

title: A bleak economic future
author: none@none.com (Shahid Mehmood)
content:
ROBERT Lucas, a towering figure of 20th-century macroeconomics and a Nobel laureate, opined on economic growth and the standard of living that “the consequences for human welfare involved in questions like these are simply staggering: once one starts to think about them, it is hard to think about anything else” (On the Mechanics of Economic Development, 1988).
The context of his observation was the significant differences in standards of living across the globe. I contemplated the same — specifically, whether our economic future might offer us some respite from our perennial failures. Sadly, it does not look good. What follows is a brief narration of various considerations that led me to this conclusion.
The incentives and structure of the economy resemble anything but a viable plan for sustained improvement in living standards and chances of shared prosperity. Tellingly, Pakistan now has the unique distinction of being the only country in the world where three different arrangements compete for a limited set of resources. The first is the formal sector, which mainly comprises an extremely unproductive and extractive public sector. The second is the ‘deep state’, growing within the bosom of the public sector (formally and informally) and meeting its growing economic interests through forced ingress. The third is the ‘informal’ sector, estimated at about 35 to 40 per cent of the formal economy, that tries its best to stay away from formality.
    
The implications of continuing this arrangement now and in the future are not well understood. There is little, if any, chance, for example, of an entrepreneur arising who could upend traditional industries and usher in economies of scale or creative disruption. It follows, then, that we will remain stuck with low-productivity, rentier industries like sugar that rely on legislative rents (taxpayer-financed subsidies) and tariff protection to shield them from competition.
The incentives and structure of the economy resemble anything but a viable plan for sustained improvement in living standards.
An even more damning predicament is the continuation of economic management as merely an accounting exercise to balance the books. From having some of the worst development indicators to the absurdity of taking foreign loans for purposes such as pension reforms, the adverse spillovers of this mediocrity are well known.
Yet one is astonished to see such pedestrian management celebrated officially. Witness the bewildering displays of vainglorious puffery under the banner of ‘nationalism’.
At the same time, trade with three of our neighbours is almost non-existent, a situation akin to a contraction of the available resource envelope and growth possibilities.
    
This attitude helps explain why we, the world’s fifth most populous country, account for less than 1pc of the massive $35 trillion global trade in goods and services.
What we have done to our human capital is another indicator of our dim prospects. Since at least the time of Adam Smith’s seminal work (1776), it has been understood that it is the most valuable input in the process of economic growth, something that Paul Romer’s endogenous growth theory (1990) put an authoritative stamp upon.
Developing this input has always remained low on our priorities. An even more grievous spectre now haunts our economy: the flight of quality human capital. It is officially celebrated as an achievement in the context of remittances. Still, no policymaker is willing to realise that the full value of quality human capital is captured outside Pakistan. Think of the innumerable examples of people who have made a name for themselves abroad. What if they had remained here and invested their time, resources, and effort to create wealth at home? Or are we just happy to receive a pittance of that effort in the form of remittances that merely sustain consumption?
The ‘Lucas critique’ of the 1970s, which transformed macroeconomics, implies that people respond to policy regimes by revising their expectations. The steady flight of skilled people from Pakistan, a trend since the 1970s, has accelerated sharply in recent decades, suggesting that citizens’ expectations of the country’s future have turned deeply pessimistic. This is reflected in what young people think. Having taught at several universities, I can attest that the majority of students view their education as a stepping stone to settling abroad.
    
For those who cannot make it to foreign shores and are active in the workforce, a difficult predicament under a poorly designed incentive structure awaits. Try justifying, logically, how in a country with one of the lowest labour force participation rates, the salaried class gets bilked for more than Rs2tr of its income in the last five years, while record inflation has decimated purchasing power for the majority. The obvious lesson (which then spills over into expectations) is that the main beneficiary of workers’ effort is the government’s coffers rather than the person. Better then to try one’s luck elsewhere.
This hollowing out, which will continue, leaves the public sector and its PSDPs as the major avenue of growth. This system spawns corruption, multi-trillion liabilities, and waste (the burden of which ultimately falls upon the taxpayer).
Lahore is the most pertinent example among Pakistani cities, with the second-largest economy and one of the highest per capita incomes. Yet it regularly tops the world’s most polluted city rankings rather than quality-of-life rankings, thanks mainly to brick-and-mortar-based PSDPs. Any material gains are more than offset by deteriorating air quality and rising health costs.
    
I can continue in this manner — for instance, by pointing out that the legislature is held hostage by the same people who have been there for at least three decades, with no meaningful economic reform emerging during their tenure. It is further compromised by their progeny, who inhabit both Houses. But I am sure the reader gets the gist of my argument: the chances that we will witness a significant turnaround in our economic fortunes are remote. We will likely remain saddled with a state whose main aim, as Marx described it, is ‘nothing else’ other than extracting taxes. At least that’s how I see it. Bob Lucas, I posit, would also have nodded in approval.
The writer is an economist. His current research focuses on the long-term analysis of various issues plaguing Pakistan’s economy, as well as economic reforms and the history of economic thought.

title: Selfhood in action
author: none@none.com (Dr Saad Malook)
content:
THE world we inhabit advances through human endeavours. To be human is to act. Idleness is a cardinal sin of humanity that causes pessimism, dehumanisation, and procrastination — postponing today’s work to tomorrow, which never comes. Idleness tends to stagnate, while action moves the world.
What causes developments in the world? Bergson believes in elan vital, Schopenhauer in the will to live, Nietzsche in will to power, and Iqbal in selfhood, each of which explains differently how humanity is driven into the future. Iqbal argues that selfhood in action causes changes in the world.
Sir Muhammad Iqbal, a philosopher of human development and action, primarily defends self-development as a means of transforming the potential for action into capability, enabling human agency to be rational, creative, productive, and moral. Iqbal’s philosophy of ‘self-development’ is actually ‘human development’, meaning people have a natural potential to develop, think, and act. To develop is to act. Surprisingly, scholars have not explored Iqbal’s philosophical oeuvre, particularly from the perspective of human development, which Pakistan desperately needs.
Action breathes life into ideas. Iqbal writes, “The Quran is a book which emphasises ‘deed’ rather than ‘idea’.” Adam, God’s vicegerent on Earth, was bestowed with infinite potential — creativity, morality, thinking, and action — transmitted to his progeny. According to Iqbal, human beings, as vicegerents, are “God’s co-workers” on the planet.
A human is not only a thinker but also an actor and a creator.
A human is not only a thinker but also an actor and a creator. Iqbal transforms the idea of Homo sapiens (human, the thinker) into Homo faber (human, the creator) and Homo actor (human, the actor). In The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam, Iqbal states, “the world is not something to be merely seen or known through concepts, but something to be made and remade by continuous action.” Making and remaking the world requires human development, a creative mind, and purposive action.
In Asrar-i-Khudi and Rumuz-i-Bekhudi, Iqbal posited his philosophy of ‘human development’. Freedom, self-respect, dignity, love, economic security, courage, education as training, and, above all, action develop the selfhood of the individual and the nation. However, unfreedom, humiliation, exploitation, hatred, economic dependency, threat, torture, and ignorance destroy the selfhood of people.
Pakistani intellectual Mahbub ul Haq advanced the idea of human development, arguing for a ‘people-first approach’ in public policy to expand people’s sociopolitical and economic choices. Like Iqbal’s, Mahbub ul Haq’s ideas also deserve attention for improving the quality of people’s lives in Pakistan.
Education is the first milestone for human development; any disorder in it means intellectual and moral decadence. The educational system in Pakistan needs revolutionary changes by appointing heads of institutions who are capable of being real agents of transformation rather than just performers on social media. Increasing the budget to promote research and incentives for researchers, and ensuring job security to stop brain drain from the profession of education are also needed.
Iqbal articulates: “Action makes life a paradise or a hell/ By nature, a human is neither an angel nor a devil.”A paradise-like life on Earth is possible only with the rule of law, justice, equal distribution of resources, and, particularly, education that fosters the freedom to flourish.
Poverty, violence, and ecological decay are pressing challenges to Pakistan and the world. Human development and action are essential to eradicating poverty — meaning that people deve­lop enough capabilities to pursue econ­o­mic activities as ent­repreneurs in IT, AI, arts, and crafts.
Peace is essential for life. Peace has two forms: negative and positive. ‘Negative peace’ is the absence of violence, mostly by force. Negative peace is short-term. ‘Positive peace’ refers to life-affirming activities through arts, literature, sports, cultural festivals, and a culture of dialogue. Positive peace is long-lasting.
A clean environment sustains life. Littering, pollution, and deforestation create health and aesthetic concerns. Reverence for the environment in individual, social, and institutional conduct is required.
Iqbal’s philosophy of human development and action can help meet crucial national and global challenges. Positively, action transforms potential into capabilities, plans into outcomes, possibilities into opportunities, pessimism into optimism, and thought into reality. Action is a supreme virtue, while idleness is a fatal vice. Let people develop and act with freedom for a better future for Pakistan.
The writer has a PhD degree from the University of Canterbury, New Zealand, and teaches philosophy at the University of the Punjab, Lahore.

title: Dead versus alive
author: none@none.com (Faisal Bari)
content:
WHEN teaching and learning are reduced to imitation, rote learning, technique, or formula, they go dead. They prevent learning from taking place. Students might be able to reproduce thoughts they’ve learned by heart, but they can’t apply that learning in real life or in places where it is supposed to help. They cannot make learning part of themselves and who they are. This type of ‘dead’ learning is shallow and doesn’t go beyond the surface. Students forget it easily too. In fact, many students say they forget the material right after exams or once the semester ends.
Movements around the world argue that schools should teach critical thinking, argumentation, debate, and reflection to support deep learning. These are essential skills and abilities that students need to develop. Curricula are designed to facilitate the development of these abilities, but when evaluations are done, we usually find mixed success. What is going wrong? When curricula are reduced to formula-based methods and techniques because teachers care more about getting through the syllabus than ensuring students engage with the learning process, the benefits become limited.
Movements around the world even argue for introducing philosophy in schools. As a subject, philosophy is generally regarded as more appropriate for older children. For the most part, it has been taught in the final years of high school or at the university level. But the Philosophy for Children (P4C) movement argues that philosophy should be introduced to younger students. There are many books on content and pedagogy in this area, and philosophy is taught in many schools.
One argument for introducing philosophy early concerns its content. People have argued that children need to be introduced to ethics and values early. Philosophy is the best way to introduce these issues, discuss them, and help students make more informed decisions. A philosophical discussion on any topic, such as racism, internet access for children, online bullying, tolerance, respect, etc., could encourage students to think about these important topics and make informed choices about who they want to be and why.
People have argued that children need to be introduced to ethics and values early.
An equally important argument for introducing philosophy in schools concerns pedagogy and what students will learn by engaging with it. Teaching philosophy is directly linked to introducing debate, argumentation, and critical and analytical thinking in classrooms. Students need to acquire and internalise these skills. For those who support this movement, philosophical discussion is an effective way to develop these skills in students.
Of course, there can be critical thinking on any theme — it does not require the subject to be from ethics or metaphysics. But since philosophy has a long tradition of debate and critical thinking, and since ethics and values need to be introduced to children, it might be easier to cultivate critical and analytical thinking through philosophy than through mathematics, physics, or languages.
But the key issue is how this is to be done. I have fond memories of my high school physics teacher, who could bring his subject to life by motivating students to approach it with curiosity, questions, and debate. He encouraged us to go deeper with each question and answer, was never impatient when we made mistakes, and was also very open to things he did not know himself. He made physics a joy to study. But in many years of schooling, I had only one such teacher in mathematics and physics, and another in language teaching. The rest — and dozens of teachers taught us over 16-odd years of schooling — were mostly trying to finish the course and give us the needed techniques and information. There was not much joy in how they taught and how we learnt.
If anecdote could be evidence, the difference with philosophy teachers was stark. When I studied philosophy at the university level, most of my professors were good at encouraging deep, critical and analytical thinking, allowing time for ambiguity and mistakes, deep learning and very deep engagement with questions. It was pure joy to be part of this experience and benefit from it. I wish every child could have access to such teachers and teaching.
Does the subject matter then? Maybe it is not the subject itself but how it is taught in our schools that has led to this difference. Most of our teachers teach languages and mathematics, especially the latter, as dead matter—something to be learned by rote, and reproduced. They do not teach it as matter that requires discovery and exploration.
In such cases, introducing philosophy might not work, as even philosophy might be limited to what Plato or Kant said rather than engaging with the subjects they discussed and thought about. Islamiat and Pakistan Studies were introduced in schools here during my student days. Both subjects were taught as content that needed only to be learnt and reproduced rather than as content requiring debate, critical analysis, and argumentation. We see the result in an almost complete lack of intellectual interest in these subjects among students.
How do we make teaching and learning alive and vibrant? By embracing debate, critical thought, and argumentation; by exposing students to ambiguity, mistakes, and open discussion; by giving them safe spaces to do so. Unfortunately, all our efforts in education — at the school or university level — in Pakistan are about content transfer, control, and reproduction. How can good thinking survive or thrive in these conditions?
The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
