title: Evolving climate architecture
author: none@none.com (Ali Tauqeer Sheikh)
content:
PAKISTAN stands at a crossroads as it prepares to attend COP31 in Turkiye next week. Every October, the Emissions Gap Report brings bad news, and every October we read it as a scorecard of how far the world is from Paris. This year, it is not a progress report. It is notice that the Paris benchmark has been breached.
The United Nations Environment Programme’s 2026 report concludes that the chance to hold warming below 1.5 degrees Celsius with no or limited overshoot “is gone”. The task now is to “minimise overshoot and return to 1.5°C”. The target survives; its meaning has flipped. No longer a ceiling, 1.5°C is a line we will cross and then try to get back under. Even the “lowest possible” overshoot peaks at 1.7 to 1.8°C.
For Pakistan, this is not abstract arithmetic. The gap between 1.5 and 1.8 is more poverty and heat in Jacobabad, wilder monsoons in Sindh, transboundary floods in Punjab, and faster glacial melt in the upper Indus. The question is simple: who pays for the overshoot years?
Just as the science matters most, the body that certifies it is going broke. For the first time in its history, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) “might not have the funds to finish an assessment report”, Nature warned recently. Contributions have fallen since 2023, and Washington has walked away. The panel needs more than CHF 20 million ($24m) to survive until 2029, less than many single-donor projects in Islamabad.
Nor can it agree on a timetable. In Addis Ababa last month, governments failed for the sixth meeting running to decide when its next reports come out. A small bloc wants the reports on emission cuts and adaptation delayed until after the 2028 global stocktake, the five-yearly review of progress under Paris. The reasons are procedural; the effect is political. For the most vulnerable countries, that delay is betrayal. Yet Pakistan, the self-declared ground zero of climate impacts, stayed away from the forum that certifies the evidence.
We need some $47bn a year to 2030 but receive under $2bn.
It is not for want of evidence. In August, the Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) published How the Climate of Pakistan Has Changed, a 45-year record and the most granular we have. Nights are warming faster than days, and springs across much of the country are up to 2.5°C warmer than in the 1980s and 1990s. Rain has become not scarcer but less dependable: the 2022 monsoon dumped up to 450 per cent above-average rain on the south, and three years later, the winter of 2024-25 brought a 67pc national deficit. That is the overshoot world in miniature.
The EU’s Paris Agreement Overshooting: Reversibility, Climate Impacts and Adaptation Needs (PROVIDE project), which studied exactly such risks, had an Islamabad partner, so the research clearly exists.
What is missing is the habit of carrying it into the rooms where global science, and therefore, global money, is decided. The empty chair reflects a deeper reflex. Pakistan’s climate diplomacy still treats finance as something to ask for: grants, owed as a moral debt by those who caused the problem. The argument is right on the merits and increasingly beside the point.
The COP29 goal of $300 billion a year is being hollowed out by the governments that pledged it, and what grant money remains goes to countries ready to absorb it. On that test, Pakistan fails. We need some $47bn a year to 2030 but receive under $2bn. The gap is not one of vulnerability but readiness.
Meanwhile, a new architecture is taking shape elsewhere, and in one corner of it Pakistan already leads. At the World Bank-IMF annual meetings in Bangkok last month, Islamabad took the chair of the Borrowers’ Platform, which gives debtors what creditors have in the Paris Club: a place to pool data, compare terms, and bargain as a bloc. On Nov 1, it also assumed the chair of the G-24, the developing-country caucus at the IMF and World Bank.
For a year then, Pakistan speaks for the debtors just as debt has become the main channel of climate finance. Disasters are paid for with borrowing, and each recovery loan makes the next shock harder to absorb.
Pakistan, where debt servicing eats 43pc of the federal budget, is itself a textbook case. Of the $10bn pledged at Geneva after the 2022 floods, about $8.7bn came from lenders. We were asked to borrow our way out of a disaster we did little to cause.
New instruments attack this chain link by link. Debt-pause clauses suspend repayments after a disaster; Grenada used one after Hurricane Beryl to defer about $30m. The V20, a bloc of finance ministers from the most climate-vulnerable countries, is building a Lifeline Fund that would pool members’ reserves into a $500m emergency facility. Africa’s new rating agency challenges unfair risk premiums; Mia Mottley’s Bridgetown Initiative demands cheaper, longer loans. Each treats climate as a balance sheet problem, and that is where the post-Paris order is taking shape.
Pakistan now heads the borrowers’ table and leaves an empty chair at the scientists’ table. The two are linked: a debtor bloc that wants climate risk priced into debt terms needs credible, nationally owned evidence, and the IPCC is where such evidence gains global standing.
Four steps follow before Antalya. First, rejoin the science table: pay into the IPCC trust fund, attend the resumed session in December, and back the least developed countries and small islands on a 2028 timeline. Second, put the PMD record to work in AR7, the next Nationally Determined Contributions, and the annual budgets. Third, trade appeals for readiness, with bankable adaptation projects, accredited national entities and climate tagging in the budget. Fourth, use the Borrowers’ Platform chair to make debt-pause clauses standard in sovereign lending and to tie debt and climate together at the stocktake.
The world has moved past the Paris target and is moving past COP as the only place where climate is decided. The winds of change are blowing elsewhere. Pakistan should stop treating COPs as tourist destinations and start engaging where the rules are written.
The writer is a climate expert.
Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

title: AI & climate adaptation
author: none@none.com (Maha Qasim, Tahreem Fatima)
content:
THIS month in Antalya, artificial intelligence will have its own day at the 31st Conference of Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The Antalya Pledge on AI asks countries to align the rapid growth of AI with global climate goals by addressing AI’s skyrocketing energy demand. The pledge requires AI companies to disclose their data centres’ energy use and shift to clean energy. The COP31 presidency has described the draft pledge as a “political” commitment on how AI is “designed, procured, powered, deployed, measured and managed” in support of climate action. However, the discussion so far has centred largely on how AI is powered rather than on how it can be leveraged to help vulnerable countries adapt to a warming world.
From extreme weather that left 87.5 million people facing acute food insecurity last year to drought draining Middle Eastern reservoirs and deadly heat in South Asia, climate change is impacting harvests, water availability, health, and livelihoods globally. AI can help communities, governments, farmers, and humanitarian organisations anticipate climate-related risks, protect essential resources, and respond faster to disasters. It can proactively convert climate data into actionable decisions that can save lives and reduce losses from adverse climate events.
AI is already proving valuable for climate adaptation. In India’s Andhra Pradesh, a pilot that sent groundnut farmers AI-based advice on the best time to sow by text message in the local language raised average yields by 30 per cent. In Bihar, communities that received AI-based flood alerts faced 30pc lower medical costs after flooding due to earlier evacuations and timely preventative health measures. In Chile, forest sensors analysed by AI detect wildfires about 12 minutes faster than traditional watchtowers. In each case, AI turned data into timely information that people could act on.
Pakistan has also taken steps in this direction. Since October 2025, the Met Office has used MAZU, a Chinese AI-based weather and early-warning system, to improve its forecasts of extreme weather. However, its nine-kilometre resolution is too coarse to capture highly localised weather such as flash floods, and Pakistan’s limited radar network restricts the local data it needs. Without such data and adequate response capacity, AI tools can produce unreliable forecasts.
AI can convert climate data into actionable decisions.
The Antalya Pledge gives Pakistan an opportunity to ensure that adaptation becomes part of the global conversation on AI and climate. To connect the AI pledge to climate adaptation, Pakistan can propose an adaptation-focused lens, with specific language on open climate data, locally adaptable AI models, and shared computing capacity — the building blocks that vulnerable countries like Pakistan need to use AI effectively. Such proposals will carry more weight if they come from many voices rather than just one.
Working through platforms such as the Climate Vulnerable Forum can allow Pakistan to build a joint position with other climate-vulnerable countries and bring their shared priorities to the climate summit’s AI day. For these commitments to be measured, reported, and funded they must be anchored in the wider climate process. Calling for the integration of AI into the Global Goal on Adaptation will ensure that AI-enabled tools are recognised in the indicators adopted at COP30 to track progress and are eligible for the tripled adaptation finance called for by 2035. At home, Pakistan’s multipronged strategy to combat climate change can include: aligning its AI policy’s sector roadmaps with the priorities of its National Adaptation Plan, str­e­ngthening its weather monitoring network, improving climate data-sharing across federal and provincial institutions, and training forecasters, resea­rchers and officials to use these tools.
At present, the global scale of planned investment in AI contrasts sharply with the persistent shortfall in climate adaptation finance. Only 32 countries host AI data centres, and Microsoft, Google, Meta and Amazon together plan to spend about $725 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026. For these countries, the pledge’s focus on clean energy matters. But for developing countries, which received just $26bn of more than the $310bn a year needed by 2035 to adapt to climate change, AI’s value as a tool for adaptation matters just as much.
Pakistan comes to Antalya with a clean energy transition shaped by its own citizens, acknowledgement of the need to accelerate clean energy, and an experience of what climate change costs. A pledge that makes AI’s power supply cleaner is a welcome step. One that also puts AI to work helping vulnerable countries adapt to climate change would make it far more meaningful.
Maha Qasim is a climate & sustainability expert. Tahreem Fatima is a sustainability professional.

title: New LPG policy
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
EACH winter, millions of working-class households across the country face the same ordeal. LPG, long considered the poor man’s fuel, is now what many middle-class families use for cooking and heating. An increasing number of homes lacking piped connections in cities end up buying cylinders as temperatures fall.
Gas rationing due to shortages caused by dwindling domestic gas reserves, together with increasing tariffs on imported RLNG, is boosting the demand for LPG. When winter sets in, demand jumps, supply tightens, and traders hoard stocks.
This year, as the petroleum minister told the National Assembly last month, the closure of the western borders has disrupted import shipments, which account for 70pc of LPG imports, exacerbating the shortages. The Saudi Aramco price, to which local LPG is linked, has also risen to $705 per tonne and the fuel is selling at Rs700-800 per kilogram — well above the official ceiling. For families already stretched by inflation, even LPG has become something to ration.
It is against this backdrop that the government has announced a new LPG policy that directs four SOEs to resume bulk imports through government-to-government and business-to-business deals. Their base prices will be published, giving the market a landed-cost benchmark.
The policy also scraps the discretionary quota system. Locally produced gas will be sold through open auctions, which should cut out the intermediaries who profit from the existing arrangement. The gap between auction proceeds and the SOEs’ import parity price will go into a dedicated fund, allowing the government to sell LPG at Rs300-350 per kilogram to BISP beneficiaries, without burdening the government budget or widening the fiscal deficit.
    
Enforcement is the weak point. It always has been. The authorities have issued many price and market rules that were never properly implemented. The Competition Commission of Pakistan, the National Explosives and Petroleum Safety Agency, and district administrations are all expected to act against collusion. They will have to be present at the retail level, where distributors have long kept the margins meant for consumers.
The auctions need watching too, since a handful of large bidders could capture them. If the policy is enforced effectively, it could potentially help end shortages and slash prices. But the question remains whether it will.
Published in Dawn, November 5th, 2026

title: Turning of the American tide
author: none@none.com (Khurram Husain)
content:
THE election results in America this week portend a sea change, and they have important ramifications for Pakistan. The Democrats have taken both the House and the Senate in a rout that reached Texas and Kansas. Anger over living costs, tariffs, and the war on Iran all played their part. For the remaining two years of his term, President Donald Trump will face a Congress armed with subpoena power and eager to use it.
This is no distant affair for us. Much of the world has spent two years trying to cope with Trump. Meanwhile, the leadership in Pakistan flamboyantly embraced him, though let’s not underestimate how well that worked. It got us lower tariffs, a White House lunch, and, above all, a central role when the Iran war needed an exit ramp. The question now is what that embrace will cost us as the man on the receiving end of it begins to lose his grip on Washington.
Pakistan has veered too close to Trump, and this might not go down well in the near future. The April ceasefire that we helped broker was a genuine achievement, and I said so at the time. The memorandum that followed in June has since collapsed, but the credit earned in those weeks still stands. Yet all of it could well come to be overshadowed by the single act of having nominated Trump for a Nobel Peace Prize in so conspicuous and overly generous a manner.
Showering the man with extravagant praise in highly public settings might have worked to win him over in the short term. But the praise kept coming long after the point had been made. In September, he was telling the UN General Assembly that our prime minister credits him with saving 30 million lives. Last month, on the day the Nobel went to someone else, the prime minister was on X lauding his “historic role” in South Asia. These things do not expire. There is a risk they get tagged onto Pakistan in the years to come, once Americans settle on their verdict of this presidency.
What looks clever in one season reads very differently at a hearing in the next.
Even more dangerous is the fact that the Trump family’s business dealings might come under congressional investigation. Reuters reported in September that probes could begin as early as February, with Trump-linked crypto firms of particular interest. Senator Richard Blumenthal, who is in line to chair an investigations panel, has promised to use his subpoena power. The same senator was asking questions about World Liberty Financial’s Pakistan deal in May last year.
If any ties lead back here, they could tie the country to the affair; the threads are already in public view. In January, our finance minister signed a memorandum with a World Liberty affiliate concerning its USD1 stablecoin. In September, the defence ministry placed a limited order with Powerus, a drone company in which two of Trump’s sons are investors. No wrongdoing has been established. The White House denies any conflict of interest, and as of July the stablecoin deal had produced no known transactions at all. But I have described that memorandum as an instrument of access, and access is exactly what investigators will want to look into. What looks clever in one season reads very differently at a hearing in the next.
These risks, however, are rooted more in optics and perceptions than in realpolitik. Pakistan’s thrust to find a place in the new regional order emerging in the Middle East must continue unabated. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, and the Tehran huddle I wrote about last week, which Field Marshal Asim Munir himself proposed, have a logic of their own that does not depend on who chairs which committee in Washington. Whatever the fallout for Pakistan, the changing of the political tide in America will be an American affair first and foremost.
The most likely outcome is that the Trump administration comes to be consumed by its wrangling with the new Congress and loses its moorings in foreign policy. A White House fighting hearings and subpoenas at home will have little bandwidth for the world.
This could produce a hazardous moment. A beleaguered and irrational president might try an adventure abroad to distract from his troubles at home, and the adventure is ready to hand. The blockade of Iran remains in place, reports in September said he saw a fresh bombing campaign as likely after the midterms, and Iran’s Supreme Leader warned on Wednesday that the war’s scope will widen if the attacks are repeated. But that seems unlikely given the stakes. This is the war voters have just punished him for, and on the eve of the vote he himself cast doubt on resuming strikes.
What is more likely is an acceleration in the pace with which America withdraws from its commitments to underwrite global order, particularly its military posture in the Middle East. I argued in April that the price of getting out of this war would be a disorderly exit from the region altogether. A Congress that owes its majority partly to anger over this war will be in no hurry to fund the next one. The Gulf monarchies have seen their American protector fail to shield them from Iranian missiles, and they are drawing their own conclusions. All this will spur the search for a new security architecture among the powers of the region, a search that will definitely include Pakistan.
Three times in our history, in the 1960s, the 1980s and the 2000s, an American embrace brought dollars and a growth spurt, and each time the money stopped when Washington’s interest moved on. This time it has brought more photographs than dollars. Ironically enough, this turning inward of the United States might just be the push Pakistan needs to learn to stand on its own feet.
The writer is a business and economy journalist.

title: Blue wave
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE politics of toxicity and confrontation at home and abroad have led to a severe setback for American President Donald Trump. His Republican Party experienced a drubbing at Tuesday’s midterm polls, with the Democrats riding a decisive blue wave to power in both houses of the US Congress, and taking control of the American government’s legislative arm.
The Democrats managed wins in deeply red states, indicating the widespread dissatisfaction with Mr Trump’s style of governance. For most Americans, the unpopular war of choice with Iran and the cost-of-living crisis it has led to were reason enough to punish the Republicans at the ballot box. Mr Trump, referring to the electoral pummelling, admitted that “part of it was Iran”.
While domestically the economy and the Trump administration’s abrasive immigration policies are likely to dominate the agenda, the rest of the world would like to know if America will change course on the foreign front.
    
In his second term, Mr Trump has turned the old international order upside down, pushed around old allies, downplayed climate change, and talked of taking over other states’ territory.
His biggest foreign folly — in partnership with Israel — has been the war against Iran. Perhaps feeling the heat, just before the midterms, Mr Trump had announced he was ending a multibillion-dollar aid programme to Israel.
It is unlikely the decision was a moral one emanating from genuine displeasure with the Zionist state’s murderous policies. More likely, it was a last-ditch attempt to court MAGA voters, many of whom increasingly question the subservience of the American political class to Israel at the expense of their own country.
In fact, expectations of a radical shift on the foreign policy front may be premature. For one, Democratic presidents, too, have launched foreign wars, and many among the supposedly ‘liberal’ party are staunch votaries of Israel. Moreover, while the Democrats will enjoy greater legislative oversight, partially limiting Mr Trump’s ability to wage and fund foreign wars, the president retains veto powers that can override Congress.
    
This means that those Democrats — and Republicans — opposed to American military action abroad must make a serious effort to halt strikes on Iran and prevent taxpayers’ dollars from funding Israel’s genocidal campaigns against the Palestinians.
While Mr Trump does not usually learn from his errors, perhaps seeing the response of the American voters he may attempt a wiser course. Candidate Trump had promised no more ‘forever wars’; President Trump must now extricate himself from a needless war he launched against Iran. It is time he heeded the call of the voters and worked on rebuilding and uniting his country, instead of destroying others.

title: The Antalya test
author: none@none.com (Jamil Ahmad)
content:
THIS year’s climate summit, to be held in Antalya next month, comes at a critical juncture. COP31 will be shadowed by UN reports that the Paris Accord target of keeping world temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius will be missed. Geopolitical tensions have compelled countries to divert attention and resources from combating climate change. With greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions on the rise, 2026 will go down as the hottest year on record. An extraordinary El Niño could worsen matters. 
For the first time in the history of the climate convention, two states, Türkiye and Australia, will share roles and responsibilities. Türkiye will have the presidency of COP and Australia has the new role of ‘president of negotiations’. Both co-hosts have been active in preparing the ground for making Antalya a success. Australia hosted a pre- COP summit in Fiji recently, with participation of leaders from the Pacific Island nations — a region most vulnerable to climate change and now also threatened by a menacing El Niño.
Türkiye has linked COP31 priorities to cities, waste and a just energy transition — three critical areas for realising Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) in developing countries and accelerating climate action. Cities account for roughly 70 per cent of global energy-related Co2 emissions. Waste, particularly food waste and landfill methane, is the third-largest source of human-caused GHG emissions globally. Yet waste management has been treated as a footnote in climate talks. Antalya has the potential to correct that, embedding circular economy principles and urban climate planning into formal UNFCCC processes. The Just Transition agenda is equally central and considered a political requisite for phasing out fossil fuels to protect households and livelihoods.
The world requires a framework for adequate and timely climate funds.
Branded as the ‘COP of implementation’, the Turkish presidency wants it to be a meeting where actions take precedence over promises, raising hopes of a breakthrough on climate finance — the main stumbling block. The previous two COP meetings took important decisions on climate finance that beg implementation. COP30 agreed to a triple adaptation fund, and decided to raise $1.3 trillion by 2035 for overall climate action. If achieved, it will be the largest fund-raiser in history for a single purpose. Unfortunately, the prospects of achieving these targets by the stipulated timeline appear bleak. The financing gap for adaptation keeps rising and is now touching $365 billion a year as per United Nations Environment Programme reports based on extrapolated needs expressed by developing countries in their NDCs and National Adaptation Plans. More worrying is the decline in international public adaptation finance flows to $26bn in 2023 from $28bn the previous year. This, according to UNEP, creates a massive funding deficit where actual adaptation needs are 12 to 14 times greater than available financial flows.
Pakistan requires huge amounts of funds for implementing its climate policies. Its NDC 3.0 submitted last year puts its total climate investment needs for 2025-2035 at $565.7bn and adaptation needs at $235.2bn, a daunting challenge for one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries, with a minimal per capita footprint of 3.2 tons. The predicament of other climate-vulnerable countries is no different. Mobilising such large funds will be impossible for the cash-strapped economies of the Global South given the complicated and lengthy processes of global financial instruments.
The world needs a robust framework that unlocks adequate, timely, and accessible funds for effective climate action in vulnerable countries. Exp­ectations from Ant­alya include est­-
­­abli­shing the imp­l­ementation str­u­cture for three significant outcomes of COP30’s Belem package. First, the two-year work pro­gra­mme to follow up the implementation of financial pledges of $1.3tr and mobilisation of $300bn by developed countries for adaptation; second, the Global Climate Finance Accountability Fram­ework to bring coherence to fragmented pledges and ensure transparency in financial disbursement; and third, the Just Transition Mechanism to support workers and communities dependent on brown industry. The Loss and Damage Fund, though operationalised, faces its first real test of replenishment at Antalya. Currently, the fund has mobilised less than $1bn — a small fraction of what is needed in this area.
While COP31 will not negotiate any new global deal, it offers an opportunity for Pakistan and other developing countries to explore options for collaboration with development partners. International support will only be effective when complemented by credible national adaptation frameworks, and a pipeline of bankable projects. 
The writer is a career diplomat, a climate expert and a former director at UNEP.
Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

title: Shrinking degree premium
author: none@none.com (Saeed Ahmed)
content:
UNIVERSITIES were originally established as centres of higher learning, places to pursue knowledge, not wages. The Abbasid-era Bayt al-Hikmah (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad brought together scholars who translated Greek, Persian, Indian, and Syriac works on philosophy, medicine, and astronomy into Arabic, and courts in Cordoba and Cairo built great libraries of their own to attract innovative thinkers. In England, the University of Cambridge has, for over 800 years, been at the centre of education, innovation, and intellectual debate, shaping some of the greatest minds in history, such as Isaac Newton, Charles Darwin, Alan Turing, Bertrand Russell, John Maynard Keynes, and Stephen Hawking. Across the Atlantic, Harvard has since at least the 19th century championed reason, research, and intellectual freedom. By the mid-20th century, its mission had widened to academic excellence, research dominance and democratic access through merit-based admission, and the university degree had become the passport to a profession.
Today’s teenagers and their parents see it differently. They pursue a degree for its economic value, and employers treat it as a signal of advanced, scarce skills. Both assumptions were long taken for granted, but both are now in doubt. Claudia Goldin and Lawrence Katz, in their work on the ‘race between education and technology’, showed that more education does not automatically meet more demand for skills. The information revolution sustained a four-decade boom in knowledge jobs, so that the graduate premium rose even as the number of graduates grew.
That long phase now appears to be ending. Recent research by José Azar, Mireia Giné, and Javier Sanz-Espín finds that the US wage premium for college graduates fell steadily between 2022 and 2026, returning to its mid-1990s level, a total drop of about eight per cent. In the UK, the FT’s John Burn-Murdoch reports a similar pattern, with a sharp fall even among STEM graduates and in London’s knowledge economy, despite a slowdown in the share of young people going to university.
What makes this striking is that it is not a story of too many graduates. Supply has levelled off in both countries, which would ordinarily push the premium up. The fall is taken as weaker demand, attributing about 28pc of it to the exposure of white-collar occupations to generative AI, although the link is not proven to be causal. Whatever the cause, the equation of academic achievement and economic value looks like the relic of a passing era.
To change how our society views skills, we need to bring them into the formal education system.
Pakistan’s own system shows the strain. The country has 278 recognised universities and degree-awarding institutions, of which 163 are public, accommodating roughly 85pc of active students. The Higher Education Commission has permitted a rapid growth of private universities, many of them thinly resourced, which enrol thousands of students for revenue, so that their graduates struggle to compete with those of elite institutions.
University enrolment, which peaked at 2.23 million, fell to about 1.96m in 2024-25, a drop of around 12pc, or more than 260,000 students, in three years. Even after eligibility criteria were relaxed, 743 of 22,300 medical and dental places remained vacant in 2025-26. The fall has been blamed on inflation, rising fees, reduced government spending, and doubts about what a degree now returns.
If the university degree is no longer the certain route to a livelihood, Pakistan needs a credible alternative, and the evidence points to skills-based training. Yet our technical and vocational education and training (TVET) sector is beset by systemic weaknesses: outdated syllabuses, poorly equipped workshops, instructors with little industry exposure, inadequate funding, and certificates that neither employers nor foreign labour markets trust. The result is a severe gap between the skills industry needs and what the system supplies.
Demand-side barriers make it worse. Because of social stigma attached to manual and technical trades, families favour academic degrees and secure government jobs that offer regular increments, pension and opportunities for corruption, so participation is low, and even lower among women. Responsibility is also divided between the federal body, National Vocational and Technical Training Commission (NAVTTC) and provincial authorities, TEVTA, producing inconsistent policies and fragmented oversight.
To change how our society views skills, we need to bring them into the formal education system on a large scale, using the network of 250,000 public and private schools and 11,000 colleges to teach skills alongside the standard curriculum. Chief ministers should champion this change and lead the effort personally. 
To bring scale and rigour to the sector, NAVTTC should evolve from a traditional regulator into a dynamic, market-driven facilitator, taking its cue from systems the world regards as vocational success stories. Germany and Switzerland train young people inside firms to standards set with industry, so that apprenticeships carry the same esteem as a degree. Germany’s ‘dual system’ splits a student’s time between vocational school and real-world company work, and the Swiss vocational system is prestigious and market responsive. Singapore’s Institute of Technical Education shows how state leadership and funding tied to employment outcomes can raise the status of technical education. 
Forging binding, legally structured partnerships, beyond MOUs, with global TVET leaders can systematically transform the entire training ecosystem. NAVTTC could partner with the Swiss Federal University for Vocational Education and Training to overhaul instructor training, adopt a German-style apprenticeship policy to build an industry-driven, dual vocational training system across Pakistan, and establish a joint venture with Singapore’s ITE Education Services to design and audit digital training centres.
A degree will remain valuable for those who can afford it and use it well. But a country cannot build its future on a credential whose price keeps rising while its worth declines. Pakistan should teach its young people the skills the economy will pay for, from the trades to communication, IT, AI, entrepreneurship and leadership, including for graduates. That would free universities from producing mass job certificates and let them return to their founding purpose: to nurture reasoning, scholarship, philosophy, innovation and the liberal arts, and to shape independent minds and original thinkers. 
The writer holds a PhD degree in economics from the University of Cambridge, and is the author of The Shady Economics of International Aid. He has served as chief economist of the State Bank of Pakistan and senior adviser at the IMF.

title: Competing demands
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE climate crisis is becoming harder to confront as the world develops new ways to consume scarce resources. At an SDPI event, Senator Sherry Rehman drew attention to the intersection of climate change, AI, energy security, and geopolitical tensions. Her concern was that governments can no longer afford to address these challenges in isolation, as decisions in one area increasingly affect another. AI, for example, is often presented as a means of improving efficiency and accelerating economic growth. Yet the data centres powering it require enormous amounts of electricity, while their cooling systems can place additional pressure on water supplies. The rapid expansion of this technology is raising questions about where the necessary energy will come from and how its environmental costs will be managed. Beyond the demands of new technology, geopolitical conflicts and uncertainty over energy supplies are also encouraging governments to prioritise immediate economic interests over emissions reduction. The latest UNEP projections suggest that existing national climate commitments, even if fully implemented, would still leave the planet heading towards approximately 2.6°C of warming by 2100. Together, these pressures are making it harder to reconcile economic priorities with the urgent need to limit global warming.
For Pakistan, these competing demands present a challenge. The country wants to attract investment in AI and digital infrastructure while struggling with expensive electricity, water shortages, and growing exposure to extreme weather. These ambitions need not be abandoned, but their resource requirements cannot be overlooked. New data centres must be assessed not simply for the investment and employment they promise but also for their impact on the power grid and local water supplies. Renewable energy could help meet demand, provided expansion is backed by reliable infrastructure. Yet the responsibility for managing these pressures cannot be equally divided. Wealthier economies have greater capacity to manage the environmental impact of digital expansion. Countries such as Pakistan, meanwhile, face climate risks with fewer resources. Integrated thinking should, therefore, shape domestic planning and global climate talks. Pakistan must press for a fairer distribution of climate responsibilities while ensuring that its own technological goals do not further strain the resources its people depend upon.
Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

title: New provinces, old solutions
author: none@none.com (Farrukh Moriani)
content:
MANY years ago, a senior official of a multilateral development bank delivered a harsh indictment of Pakistan’s state of affairs: it is a seriously large country run by a succession of non-serious policymaking elite. While the setting for the delivery of this critique was an informal one, it left one pondering its accuracy. Sadly, Pakistan’s ruling elites, irrespective of the political flag they bear, regularly try and prove the gentleman right. The recent spate of political statements on the creation of new provinces serves as an example.
    
Administrative boundaries are not sacrosanct and must be viewed as mechanisms designed to serve evolving and defined public interest. Speaking about the creation of new provinces is not, therefore, tantamount to a conspiracy. Rather it reflects a healthy approach to reassessing their utility and viability.
That said, restructuring a federation is not a trifling matter as its implications run deep and wide — from the obvious fiscal imperatives and changes to the balance of political representation, to the everyday impact on public service delivery and on the lives of citizens. Hasty, discordant political sound bites cannot, therefore, be a substitute for rigorous, extensive, and inclusive deliberation and analysis.
The experience of other nations in this respect, including several where the author has had the privilege of leading the process, is instructive. There are two common strands of note.
First, there is no single model to follow and changes are rooted in legal, political, and economic contexts. Second, political motives aside, each effort identified specific problems that the change was intended to solve.
India’s establishment of Telangana was characterised by strong institutional arrangements, and extensive public engagement over an 11-month period. Brazil’s division of Goiás to form Tocantins responded to a long-standing public movement and leveraged constitutionally mandated plebiscitary mechanisms for public consent. In Russia, consolidation rather than fragmentation served as the principle for establishing the Zabaykalsky Krai region, with improved living standards being a clearly defined objective. Accelerating socioeconomic development was also the raison d’être for Timor-Leste’s establishment of the world’s newest Special Administrative Region in Oé-Cusse.
From these and other global experiences, one can distill several insights and lessons for Pakistan.
Lesson 1: Never treat the issue of creating new regions as merely redrawing the map. This reductive approach will upend any potential benefits that might accrue from a careful and considered process of reviewing how government is structured. The era of arbitrary, extractive cartography — for example, the Radcliffe Line, the Sykes-Picot Agreement, and Cecil Rhodes’s British South Africa Company — is dead and should stay that way. Pakistan should frame the issue of new provinces not as a form of territorial re-engineering but as a fundamental state reform aimed at reducing inequality, democratising economic and developmental opportunities, and improving public services.
Lesson 2: Defined public interest, as opposed to political ambition or the facilitation of vested interests, should be the principal driver for change. Deep and genuine engagement with the public, not just their representatives, must constitute the starting point, not the finish line, and be non-negotiable. Furthermore, a distinction must be made between public need — the genuine reasons which justify change — and public demand — which can be easily manufactured through weaponising algorithms and orchestrated street power. The stronger the mechanisms for filtering out political noise and faux narratives, the greater the likelihood of neutralising proxy gerrymandering on public opinion.
Administrative boundaries are not sacrosanct and must be viewed as mechanisms designed to serve evolving and defined public interest.
Lesson 3:There needs to be absolute clarity on the purpose of the proposed changes, an agreement on the precise problems the changes set out to resolve, and complete transparency on plans. Vague, stylised assertions around improving governance and service delivery, and absence of transparency on both purpose and process, will only serve as a petridish for political and social discontent and extended, simmering disputes.
    
Three other insights, peculiar to Pakistan’s context are important to highlight: first, the functionalisation and empowerment of local governments must be embedded within the debate on new provinces, as these are not mutually exclusive discussions.
Second, it is necessary to look under the hood of how provinces themselves create administrative units, based as they are on administrative fiat rather than legislative approval — otherwise, we risk repeating the mistake made under the 18th Amendment’s Article 140-A, which left it to the provinces to establish independent local governments (they didn’t).
Third, rejigging old solutions wrapped inside tired narratives and tactics (administrative fiat, holding illegal/ mala fide referendums, relying heavily on ethno-linguistic nationalism as a criterion) will be unfortunate.
To move forward, a three-step roadmap is proposed:
1: Establish a ‘Commission for Citizen-Centric Change’ as a multi-stakeholder, cross-party, independent, and empowered institutional arrangement to lead the process. As part of its work, it should be tasked with extensive public engagement, and the conduct of technical analysis to determine criteria, weigh options, and ensure transparency and knowledge management.
2: Institute a three-dimensional ‘Public Interest Test’ framework that includes an assessment of the public benefits and whether they meet citizen aspirations and socioeconomic needs; a fiscal viability review to determine financial and economic sustainability; and an institutional readiness mapping to measure state capabilities and agility.
3: Test this framework and institutional arran­gements by targeting one province. Punjab is the most obvious case for review given its size and the ongoing debate on a south Punjab province. It should be used as a policy lab. Results emerging from this lab should inform a nationwide scaling.Indeed, it is time to get serious.
The writer is a former adviser to the chair of the G77 and China.

title: Electoral reform
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE parliamentary committee on electoral reform, which is being constituted by the National Assembly Speaker, sounds promising. But the public has watched this exercise many times before. None has delivered a credible election. Therefore, the legislators must ask why the laws already on the books keep failing before they start redrafting new statutes.
Pakistan’s current electoral framework appears to be sound. The Election Commission of Pakistan enjoys constitutional protection, financial autonomy, and a bipartisan process for appointing its leadership. Yet both the 2018 and 2024 general elections ended in bitter disputes over the credibility and transparency of results.
Neither the government nor the opposition has made a serious effort to initiate consultations on a replacement for the current chief election commissioner whose tenure ended nearly two years ago.
The real problem is the gulf between the statute book and what happens on polling day, not the laws. Legitimacy depends on consistent enforcement, genuine institutional independence, and a shared willingness to respect the rules.
    
Nevertheless, the committee can still close several gaps in the current legislation.
First, provinces routinely delay local government elections for years, citing the need to amend local laws. This stops the ECP from discharging its constitutional duty when the term of an elected LG expires. Parliament should bar provincial governments from altering local election laws once a council completes its tenure, so that the ECP can hold polls within the constitutional time frame.
Second, campaign finance rules are full of loopholes. Under the Elections Act, 2017, candidates can dodge spending limits by claiming that third-party expenditure was not authorised by their campaigns. Spending limits mean little if a candidate can disown whoever spends on their behalf. If money is spent to advance a candidate’s campaign, the candidate should answer for it.
Third, financial scrutiny must be extended to foreign funding to both parties and individual candidates routed through affiliated non-profits and offshore accounts for the sake of transparency.
    
Last but not least, the caretaker government model needs an overhaul. Letting political parties haggle over nominees does not guarantee neutrality, which must be tested against the record of those appointed. The law should have clearer safeguards against conflicts of interest and political bias among caretaker officeholders, so that transitions are not open to partisan interference.
These fixes are worth making. But they will count for little if meddling in polls and selective enforcement continue to be unchecked.
Domestic and international observers raised serious concerns about the 2024 results process. Until parliament deals with the interference that feeds public distrust, further amendments will change very little.
The country does not need a new rulebook. It needs institutions and actors who follow the one it already has.
Published in Dawn, November 4th, 2026

title: Seeing red in Iran
author: none@none.com (Mahir Ali)
content:
IN the run-up to yesterday’s US mid-term elections, it became obvious that, almost four decades after the Cold War ended, the ‘spectre of communism’ Marx and Engels identified in the 19th century still haunts Western consciousness.
Islamophobia might have been the most prominent weapon, but it was accompanied by diatribes against Marxists and communists, invariably directed against people who are neither. For good measure, some of them are simultaneously derided as Islamist jihadists.
The American establishment’s obsession with the communist threat, real or imagined, dates back to the early 20th century, and has served as a guiding principle of its foreign (and domestic) policy since the Truman era. One of the CIA’s first interventions, against Iranian democracy in the early 1950s, was justified as a blow against communist influence, even though the popular nationalist Mohammad Mossadegh was barely left of centre. Furthermore, the communist party Tudeh had initially misidentified him as a mole for US interests, recognising only belatedly that his oil nationalisation was in Iran’s interest.
The party was decimated in the wake of the CIA-guided coup that re-established the Shah’s reign, under the aegis of Savak, MI6, and Mossad. The survivors fled abroad, mostly ending up in East Germany, although many underground operatives remained in situ, and retained some influence in the military arm of the state. Thus, when Tudeh resurfaced in the lead-up to the 1979 revolution, it wasn’t starting from scratch. It participated in the mass surge against the tyrannical Shah, but, unlike the militant Mujahideen-i-Khalq and others on the left, acknowledged the Khomeini phenomenon as a legitimate expression of the popular will.
That helps to explain why Tudeh briefly became the main opposition in a milieu dominated by the Islamic Republican Party. It’s unlikely this arrangement would anyhow have lasted long, but things came to a head in 1982-83. 
The US today faces its own Great Game fallout.
The saga is laid out in entertaining detail in espionage specialist author Ben Macin­t­yre’s recently published Redwood — a fascinating, albeit somewhat breathless, account of the defection in Tehran of a senior KGB officer, Vladimir Kuzichkin, the Soviet point man for contacts with Tudeh and a network of spies. In Macintyre’s reading, Kuzichkin was disillusioned with his corrupt colleagues, as well as with the Soviet polity, but above all, it was his impotence that drove him to risk approaching MI6, expecting Western medicine to offer a cure. (Viagra was more than a decade away, but MI6 was able to organise a discreet circumcision.)
More significantly, Kuzichkin passed on to MI6’s Ian McCredie his list of Iranian contacts and details of communications with Moscow. MI6 shared them with the CIA, which was unable to operate in Iran at the time, and the latter insisted on sharing them with Iran’s intelligence agencies. Iran had only recently released the hostages taken at the US embassy, but while the American cold warriors might not have been fans of the clergy, in their blinkered worldview the communist threat was paramount. MI6 was happy, as always, to play second fiddle. The suspicion was that Moscow’s arms and gold were preparing Tudeh for a coup that could pave the way for a Soviet invasion, as in Afghanistan, and further tilt the Cold War imbalance towards communism.
By 1982, it should have been obvious to Moscow that the Afghan occupation was going awry — thanks largely to the CIA’s covert war via Pakistan. Macintyre does not mention Zbigniew Brzezinski’s role, through the CIA and regional assets, in luring the Red Army into its biggest folly. But, giv­en the state of aff­airs in the nei­­ghb-ourhood, it’s unl­ikely Moscow wou­ld seriously have contemplated a sim­ ilar misadventure in Iran. Non­etheless, it was decided to impart Redwood’s information to the Iranian authorities, and the chosen venue was Islamabad, courtesy of the then ISI chief Gen Abdul Rehman Akhtar.
Even though senior elements of the Iranian leadership — including Ayatollah Khomeini, parliamentary speaker Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, and prime minister Mir-Hossein Mousavi — had their doubts about the imminence of a communist coup attempt and advised restraint, the president Ali Khamenei and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps chief Mohsen Rezaei favoured haste, leading to thousands of arrests and mass executions, alongside torture and televised ‘confessions’. As in Afghanistan earlier this century, the US is today confronted, in part, with the consequences of its own Great Game machinations. But ask any surviving cold warrior, and most likely they’ll still contend it was a price worth paying for keeping the world safe from communism. Many of us, meanwhile, awaiting this week’s election results, look forward to the impending demise of the American empire.

title: Storage deficit
author: none@none.com (Srraa Tahir)
content:
THE Strait of Hormuz closed on Feb 28, 2026. Within days, QatarEnergy declared force majeure.
Pakistan, which sourced almost all its LNG from Qatar, asked Saudi Arabia to reroute crude through the Red Sea and released gas it had been holding back for weeks. There was no gas storage and very little oil storage to fall back on, because none had ever been built.
The timing made it worse. Years earlier, Pakistan signed long-term LNG contracts. Then IMF-driven tariff changes made gas too expensive for industries running captive power plants, and they switched to solar. Demand fell just as the country was locked into more gas than it needed. The pipelines reached the capacity threshold and the authorities curtailed up to 350 mmcfd of domestic gas. Then the strait closed, Qatari cargoes were stranded, and the curtailed fields had to be switched back on within weeks. Too much gas, then too little, and no storage to manage either.
    
This is not a new problem. Policymakers have known for decades that Pakistan needs oil and gas storage, but have done little about it.
Gas storage works by pumping surplus gas into depleted reservoirs when demand is low and drawing it back out when supply runs short.
As early as 2004, an ADB study examined 107 locations and recommended two depleted fields in Badin, and a 2022 study added a third. Exploration companies operate these fields and could convert them, but no commercial model has been settled. A guaranteed return for investors, the model that inflated power costs for two decades, would be a mistake. It paid for capacity whether used or not, and gave sponsors little reason to control costs.
Competitive bidding works the other way: developers compete on the fee they charge to store and return gas, overrun risk stays with them, and the state only sets the terms. Feasibility tenders were issued in 2024 and again in 2026, a month before the strait closed. Even then, the first facility will cover only 11 to 12 days of consumption, against the month officials say is needed.
Oil storage has failed for its own reasons. The main one is that no one is paid to hold it. Marketing companies must keep 20 days of cover, but prices are revised every fortnight, so extra stock risks a loss whenever prices fall, and the pricing formula does not recover the cost of tanks. Most companies stay near the minimum, and the state has never built a strategic reserve of its own.
Pakistan needs oil and gas storage.
The idea of letting foreign suppliers hold fuel in Pakistan was first floated in 2015. In 2023, the government approved it: suppliers could keep product in bonded storage without paying duty, pay only when they sold locally, and re-export freely. Not one supplier has used it — for three reasons.
First, the rules require a foreign supplier to register a presence in Pakistan. Large traders are used to storing oil in places like Fujairah in the UAE or Singapore without opening an office there. Asking them to do so here adds cost and paperwork for little benefit. Second, nothing guarantees a supplier can take its oil back out. A future government facing a shortage could block exports, just when it would want to sell elsewhere. Third, five bodies have a say: customs, the regulator, the State Bank, and the commerce and petroleum ministries. Each writes its own rules, and no one makes them fit together.
The current government has reopened the policy, an admission that it has attracted no investment.
    
The strait showed that fuel stored in the Gulf can be cut off without warning. Fuel held in Pakistan by foreign suppliers, available for local sale, would give the country a cushion next time. The fix requires detail, not reinvention. The rules must state who can take part without a Pakistani company, how ownership changes when part of a tank is sold, how banks process those sales, and which single office settles disputes. Traders choose where to store oil based on how fast licences come and whether rules stay stable. Fujairah attracts traders not because its government built the tanks, but because it made storage simple and predictable.
In both cases, the government need not spend its own money. Its job is to write clear rules, issue licences quickly, and honour its commitments.
Pakistan has paid for the lack of storage twice this year, first with more gas than it could use, then with too little. The gas sites were identified over 20 years ago; the oil policy has existed for years. What has been missing is the will to follow through.
Hormuz will not be the last disruption, and if storage is not ready before the next one, the cost will again fall on industry, on households, and on a treasury paying premium prices for emergency cargoes. The next closure will not wait for another feasibility study.
The writer is a corporate lawyer working in the energy and infrastructure sector across the Middle East and Pakistan.
Published in Dawn, November 3rd, 2026

title: Pakistan’s G-24 role
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S new role as chair of G-24 comes at a crucial moment for the Global South. Developing nations are struggling to navigate an era defined by steep tariffs, a revival of industrial policy, weakening multilateralism, rising interest rates, escalating inflation, climate shocks, and global conflicts that have shaken the world economy. And yet, its new position offers Islamabad an opportunity to articulate the concerns of developing economies, build consensus on a common development agenda, and push for a more equitable global financial and economic order. It is a mandate to lead the developing world effectively and to work closely with major powers on critical reforms across international financial institutions. Achieving this will not be easy. For decades, the global financial framework — dominated by the Bretton Woods institutions — has largely served Western economies, while developing nations are asked to shoulder the costs of global macroeconomic volatility while facing disproportionately higher borrowing costs and severe capital constraints.
By stepping into its new role, Islamabad assumes the responsibility of presenting these shared grievances as a cohesive agenda for structural change. Central to this effort is redefining how Western economic powers view the developing world. The focus must shift from seeing developing nations as vulnerable economies in need of more debt or debt relief to recognising their contributions to global economic growth. As the finance minister highlighted, the focus must shift to the “immense potential of emerging and developing nations as drivers of investment, innovation, entrepreneurship, and global growth”. Achieving reform will require bridging the gap between rhetoric and policy action. Key priorities for the G-24 mandate must include advocacy for expanded and easier access to concessional financing, an end to tariff-led industrial policies, the revival of multilateralism, and streamlined mechanisms for debt reduction. The traditional economic narrative that places Western financial centres at the core while relegating developing markets to the periphery is no longer sustainable in an interconnected world economy. As the finance minister has noted, the future of developing economies is central to the future of the global economy. While sweeping changes are unlikely to materialise entirely during Pakistan’s tenure, Islamabad has a crucial window to push this debate to the centre of the global reform agenda.
Published in Dawn, November 3rd, 2026

title: Learning from polio
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE eighth polio case of 2026, involving a 13-month-old girl from Khyber’s Bara tehsil, raises an important question for Pakistan’s eradication programme: how much does it learn from each child who becomes infected? Six of this year’s eight cases have emerged in KP, while sewage samples from the Peshawar-Khyber corridor continue to test positive. The virus is circulating despite repeated campaigns. The latest drive, running from Nov 2 to 8, aims to vaccinate nearly 24m children in 97 districts. Such efforts are essential, and the fall in cases this year is encouraging. But the programme must also explain why infections continue to surface in places where vaccination has been repeatedly undertaken. Was the child missed during earlier rounds? Were doses incomplete, or did the family move between districts? Did local surveillance identify the danger early enough? These questions must be investigated without assigning blame to families or front-line workers before the facts are known.
There is a wider issue of accountability. The authorities announce campaign targets and impressive vaccination totals, but the public hears far less about what investigations uncover after a confirmed case. Health managers should publish clear findings on vaccination histories, gaps in coverage, and the corrective steps taken. Positive environmental samples should trigger documented follow-up in affected neighbourhoods, with results reviewed before the next campaign. This would help distinguish problems of access from weaknesses in delivery, and direct resources where they are needed most. Routine immunisation at clinics must also be reinforced so that a child’s protection does not depend entirely on the next emergency drive. Balochistan’s absence of reported cases since November 2024 is welcome, though continuing transmission across the Afghan border makes vigilance necessary. Pakistan has already shown that it can mobilise millions of doses and thousands of vaccinators. It now needs to demonstrate that lessons from every infection are being used to prevent the next one.

title: GM seed governance - lessons from cotton
author: News Desk
content:
Genetically modified (GM) seed technology has improved agricultural productivity, pest management and climate resilience globally. Bt cotton is a GM variety containing a gene from the soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) that protects against bollworms, reducing the need for insecticides. Pakistan formally commercialised Bt cotton in 2010 as its only widely adopted GM crop.

Yet despite Bt cotton accounting for an estimated 95% of the country's cotton area by 2022, national cotton production has fallen to a 40-year low. While many factors have contributed to this decline, including pests beyond Bt cotton's targeted bollworms, diseases such as Cotton Leaf Curl Virus, climate change and evolving crop economics; weaknesses in GM seed governance remain an important part of the story. This insight examines Pakistan's GM seed governance through the case of Bt cotton.

GM crops have been commercially cultivated since 1996 and, by 2025, were grown in 30 countries on 216 million hectares. GM cotton accounted for 76.7% of global cotton area, with Pakistan in fifth place. Yet large-scale adoption has not translated into sustained gains. India offers a useful regional comparison given similar adoption timelines and production systems.

India's cotton yield more than doubled from 191 kg/ha in 2002 to 440 kg/ha in 2024, reaching 511 kg/ha in 2016. Pakistan initially recorded a substantially higher yield of 622 kg/ha and peaked at 815 kg/ha in 2011, but subsequently experienced considerable volatility, falling to 390 kg/ha in 2022 before recovering to 590 kg/ha in 2024. Consequently, Pakistan's initial yield advantage over India narrowed substantially, suggesting that its early productivity streak was not sustained.

Bt cotton, based largely on Monsanto's first-generation Cry1Ac (MON531) technology, entered Pakistan informally around 2002, before effective systems for biosafety, variety registration and seed quality assurance were in place. By 2007, an estimated 60% of Pakistan's cotton area was already planted with unregulated Bt cotton. Despite formal commercialisation in 2010, regulatory oversight struggled to catch up with the established informal market. By 2012, 52 Bt varieties were being cultivated, but only nine were officially approved. Around 85% of seed samples had an unknown origin and only 1% met the required Bt toxin level.

Consequently, these factors increased Bt-targeted pest resistance and secondary pests, pushing farmers back towards pesticide use. Cotton area declined from 3.2 million hectares in 201415 to 1.9 million hectares by 2025, with pink bollworm alone estimated to cause annual losses of around one million bales. Furthermore, first-generation Cry1Ac technology remained widely used even as its effectiveness declined.

The experience also highlighted the importance of conserving cotton's genetic diversity. Studies found a narrow genetic base among cultivated varieties in Pakistan, while gene flow between Bt and non-Bt cotton was documented in Faisalabad. These findings raise concerns about cross-contamination and the long-term preservation of indigenous varieties and genetic resources essential for future breeding.

Pakistan has introduced a series of reforms to strengthen GM seed governance. Together, they provide a stronger institutional foundation than existed during the early years of Bt cotton adoption. However, important gaps remain.

The first gap is institutional coordination. GM crops must complete two separate regulatory processes: biosafety approval by the National Biosafety Committee (NBC) and seed certification and variety registration by the National Seed Development & Regulatory Authority (NSDRA). Yet, neither the Pakistan Biosafety Rules 2005 nor the Seed (Amendment) Act 2024 explicitly establishes a formal mechanism for coordination or information-sharing between the two authorities. A joint coordination mechanism could ensure that biosafety approval, seed certification and post-release oversight inform one another throughout a GM variety's lifecycle.

The second gap concerns post-release monitoring. While institutions such as the Pakistan Central Cotton Committee (PCCC) generate technical evidence, provincial agriculture departments are better placed to monitor crops in the field and identify local changes in crop performance and pest pressure. A formal linkage between provincial field monitoring, research institutions and NSDRA could ensure that such evidence informs national seed regulation and future approvals.

The third gap is research capacity. Sustained research and resistance monitoring are essential to maintaining GM crops' effectiveness. Globally, documented cases of practical resistance to Bt crops rose from three in 2005 to 16 by 2016. Pakistan's constrained agricultural research funding, including financial challenges at PCCC, underscores the need for stable funding for varietal evaluation, resistance monitoring and preservation of genetic diversity.

GM maize is the next test for Pakistan's seed governance. Maize covers 1.59 million hectares, with production estimated at 8.79 million tonnes in 202526. Unlike Bt cotton, which spread informally before effective regulation, GM maize is now being considered through a government-led commercialisation framework, with coexistence of GM and non-GM maize under discussion.

Safeguards should therefore be established before widespread adoption, including traceable seed, post-release monitoring and a clear biosafety framework. Designated cultivation zones, alongside appropriate isolation distances, could further limit cross-contamination between GM and non-GM maize, protecting non-GM production and preserving genetic diversity.

In conclusion, Pakistan's Bt cotton experience shows that technological adoption without strong governance can limit long-term gains. As GM agriculture expands, Pakistan must strengthen regulation, monitoring, research and stewardship before adoption outpaces oversight.

Lessons from Bt cotton must inform the commercialization of GM maize, advocating for proactive safeguards like traceable seeds, robust biosafety frameworks, and designated cultivation zones to prevent cross-contamination.

title: Climate diagnosis
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE Lancet Countdown’s latest findings should change how Pakistan thinks about illness as much as how it thinks about climate change. The report estimates that heat contributed to 710,000 deaths worldwide in 2023. In Pakistan, a patient arriving at a clinic with dehydration, kidney injury or breathing difficulties may be experiencing the effects of extreme weather without that connection ever entering the medical record. A child treated for diarrhoea after flooding, or an elderly person whose heart condition deteriorates during prolonged heat, becomes another isolated case rather than part of a wider pattern. The result is a dangerous knowledge gap. Without reliable information on where climate-related illnesses occur, who is most affected and how many lives are lost, health authorities cannot judge the scale of the problem. Climate change is already altering the demands placed on medicine; Pakistan’s healthcare planning has yet to catch up.
This is where the warning from former health officials deserves closer attention. Rather than producing another catalogue of vulnerabilities, the government should begin with what hospitals and clinics can actually record, diagnose and treat. Provincial health departments could require major facilities to track heatstroke, dehydration, acute kidney injury and other conditions aggravated by extreme weather, with data reviewed alongside local temperature and rainfall trends. Primary-care staff need practical guidance for recognising heat illness early, especially among children, older people and patients taking medicines that affect hydration. Hospitals should examine whether their emergency departments can cope with seasonal surges, and whether essential treatment can continue when power or water supplies fail. None of this requires waiting for another international declaration. It requires health officials to treat climate exposure as a routine part of patient care. Public reporting would also reveal which districts lack the staff, equipment and referral arrangements to respond. Pakistan has spent years describing itself as vulnerable to climate change. The Lancet findings present a more immediate challenge: can its health system identify the people being harmed, offer them treatment and learn enough from their cases to prevent avoidable deaths?

title: Without consequence
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
JOURNALISTS today face ever more sophisticated threats, while those who target them continue to walk free. From drone attacks to online harassment and legal intimidation, the methods of silencing reporters are multiplying, with little fear of punishment. This year’s International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists, observed today, carries the theme ‘Threats Evolve. Impunity Endures’. According to Unesco, 189 journalists were killed in 2024 and 2025, most of them in conflict zones. Yet justice remains elusive in the vast majority of cases. The global impunity rate has risen to 86pc, the first increase since Unesco began measuring it in 2012. This failure to punish those responsible sends a dangerous message: journalists can be attacked or killed without fear of consequence. 
Gaza shows what happens when those responsible are not held to account. The Committee to Protect Journalists recorded 129 journalists killed worldwide in 2025, with Israel responsible for two-thirds of the deaths. In August that year, Israeli strikes on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital killed 22 people, including five journalists. An AP investigation published a year later found that nobody had been held accountable. For Palestinian journalists, who have been reporting a war largely closed to foreign media, the dangers are especially severe. Their deaths leave the outside world with fewer people able to document what is happening. Similarly, in Sudan and Ukraine, journalists risk their lives exposing the horrors of war, while those who target them often escape justice. Without independent investigations and punishment for those found responsible, promises to protect journalists will remain empty.
Pakistan’s record is also deeply troubling. Freedom Network’s latest report documents threats and assaults against journalists, along with 45 cases of legal action or threatened prosecution. The growing use of Peca against journalists investigating official wrongdoing is particularly worrying. Repeated summonses, seized devices and costly court battles are enough to silence a reporter even without a conviction. The human cost of this failure is evident in the case of journalist Mudassar Mahmood Naru. Eight years after his disappearance, his son is growing up without a father and his family is still waiting for answers. The laws meant to protect journalists offer little comfort when the bodies responsible for enforcing them fail to act. In smaller towns, where reporters have fewer resources, intimidation often goes unreported. The state must ensure that attacks are properly investigated, protection bodies function and cybercrime laws are not used to punish legitimate reporting. A country where journalists fear telling the truth more than wrongdoers fear being exposed has its priorities wrong.

whyMatters: This article is crucial for competitive exam students as it provides contemporary data and arguments regarding media freedom, human rights, and state accountability. summary: Journalists globally face escalating and sophisticated threats, including drone attacks, online harassment, and legal intimidation, with a worrying increase in impunity for perpetrators.

The global impunity rate for crimes against journalists has risen to 86%, indicating a dangerous failure to hold perpetrators accountable and sending a message that journalists can be attacked without consequence.

Conflict zones like Gaza, Sudan, and Ukraine exemplify this impunity, with Israel being responsible for a significant number of journalist deaths in 2025, leading to a critical lack of independent documentation from these areas.

Pakistan's record is equally troubling, marked by legal intimidation (e.g., PECA misuse), physical assaults, and enforced disappearances, underscoring the state's failure to ensure investigations and protect legitimate reporting.

Freedom Network's latest report for Pakistan documented 45 cases of legal action or threatened prosecution against journalists.
Journalist Mudassar Mahmood Naru disappeared eight years ago, with his family still awaiting answers.
