title: Spirit of cooperation
author: none@none.com (Pernille Ironside)
content:
FOR almost 80 years, Pakistanis have served under the UN flag, helping communities recover from conflict and rebuild peace. Pakistan has also provided refuge to millions fleeing instability. Pakistan has helped make international cooperation possible. Today, that spirit matters more than ever. Countries may disagree on politics, economics, and security, but share challenges none can resolve alone. Cooperation protects national interests.
The UN secretary-general’s message was clear during his recent visit to Pakistan: no country can tackle interconnected challenges alone. Conflict disrupts trade and raises food and energy costs; climate change threatens water, agriculture and livelihoods; pandemics and artificial intelligence bring cross-border risks and opportunities.
For Pakistan, these connections are not theoretical. The devastating floods of 2022 caused an estimated $30 billion in damage and economic losses, with women and children among those facing the most lasting consequences. The floods of 2025 brought another reminder of the human and economic costs of climate-related disasters. Building resilience requires strong national leadership, effective domestic resource allocation, and better development of vulnerable communities, but also international solidarity, climate finance, and partnerships.
Pakistan’s recent diplomacy offers another illustration. The secretary-general praised Pakistan’s role in facilitating dialogue between the United States and Iran. Such efforts cannot guarantee peace, but they show why diplomacy matters: even when interests diverge sharply, keeping channels open can create possibilities that confrontation alone cannot.
Pakistan’s contribution to UN peacekeeping and its long-standing role in hosting refugees reflect the same understanding. A more peaceful region, functioning international institutions, and respect for international law matter directly to Pakistan’s security and prosperity. 
What are countries choosing to do about a divided world?
The stakes are also domestic. Pakistan’s population of around 255 million includes a vast young generation. Realising its potential depends on access to quality education, relevant skills, and decent work. Turning demographic scale into an economic dividend requires sustained national investment and international partnership. Women and girls, people with disabilities, and other marginalised groups must be able to shape and share in that opportunity; otherwise, inequality will hold back progress.
Defending multilateralism does not mean defending every aspect of today’s institutions. Many people question whether international cooperation can deliver solutions to the problems they face in daily life. Those concerns deserve to be taken seriously. The answer is not less multilateralism, but better multilateralism: more effective, more representative and better equipped to deliver. 
The secretary-general’s UN80 initiative is part of that effort. But reform is a shared responsibility: Member states should provide the political leadership and resources needed to make cooperation work, while holding the UN accountable for delivering on its mandates.
The UN Charter’s principles remain essential: sovereign equality, peaceful settlement of disputes, international law, and human rights. They are not always upheld consistently. That is a reason to demand greater accountability, not discard them. When rules apply selectively, trust erodes and every country is more exposed.
Weaker cooperation has real consequences: lives lost to conflict and disaster, livelihoods destro­y­­ed, girls pushed out of school and opportunities denied to yo­­ung people. The UN provides a place to negotiate, coordina­­te action, and supp­ort people facing crises. It cannot resolve every conflict, but can help keep dialo­gue open and turn commitments into results.
Pakistan’s commitment to the multilateral system was also recognised when President Asif Ali Zardari conferred the Nishan-i-Imtiaz on Secretary-General Guterres on Oct 6 — the first time Pakistan has bestowed the honour on a serving UN secretary-general. It recognised his service and the long-standing Pakistan-UN partnership.
On United Nations Day, the question is not whether the world is divided. It plainly is. The question is what countries choose to do about it. In a world where we cannot control every change taking place around us and so many challenges cross borders, we can choose whether to meet the challenge through confrontation or cooperation; division or dialogue; unilateralism or solidarity.
For Pakistan, as for every country, cooperation, dialogue and solidarity are not concessions of sovereignty. They are investments in a more stable, sustainable and prosperous future. 
The writer is United Nations resident coordinator (ad interim) in Pakistan.
Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

title: Beyond tariff cuts
author: none@none.com (Ehsan Malik)
content:
PAKISTAN cannot build a competitive industry by protecting it indefinitely. Nor can reducing protection, by itself, turn domestic manufacturers into exporters. Tariffs shape investment decisi­o­­ns, but competitiveness also depends on energy, te­­­chnology, scale, supply chains, market access, and security. A credible industrial strategy must address them together. Unconditional protection raises prices, blunts incentives to innovate, and rewards selling to a captive home market. Consu­mers finance inefficiency, and capital chases protected returns rather than export opportunities. Where there is no credible prospect of competitiveness, protection merely postpones adjustment at public expense.
The National Tariff Policy 2025-30, therefore, points broadly in the right direction. Fewer tariff slabs, cheaper imported inputs, and phased elimination of additional customs and regulatory duties can lower costs and reduce the bias against exports. But these are instruments of competitiveness, not substitutes for the conditions that make exports possible.
The essential complement is a measurable programme to cut the costs the state imposes on production. If manufacturers face a timetable for lower protection, the government should face one for affordable, reliable energy, prompt tax refunds, simpler regulation, and efficient logistics. Otherwise, industry is asked to adjust while the state’s own contribution to uncompetitiveness goes unaddressed. This is not an argument for waiting until every domestic problem is solved; that would make protection permanent. It is a case for distinguishing activities with little prospect of competitiveness, those capable of achieving it, and a narrow set of strategic capabilities.
The polyester chain shows the cost of failing to draw these distinctions. The textile industry association, APTMA, argues that protection on polyester staple fibre and its key input, purified terephthalic acid, raises costs for downstream textiles, while the country’s sole PTA plant, commissioned in 1998, lags newer plants in China and India. These claims by interested users warrant independent examination.
The test is straightforward. Has prolonged support delivered globally competitive costs, technological upgrading, and lower energy use per tonne? Has it helped downstream producers compete in synthetic and blended textiles? Protection that preserves an inefficient input supplier while handicapping a much larger export opportunity defeats its own purpose. Energy illustrates the shared responsibility. High electricity tariffs and excessive electricity consumption are different problems: the government must fix the first; manufacturers must invest to reduce the second. Consumers and downstream exporters should not indefinitely finance either failure.
Protection that preserves an inefficient input supplier while handicapping a much larger export opportunity defeats its own purpose.
Yet an equally indiscriminate withdrawal of support could destroy capabilities with a viable future. Auto parts deserve assessment on this basis. Complaints about expensive vehicles and meagre exports obscure engineering skills within the supplier base. Toolmaking, casting, machining, moulding, process control, and quality assurance are not tied to one vehicle. Partnerships with foreign manufacturers can develop capabilities serving replacement markets, other engineering industries, and, where specifications permit, defence production.
These capabilities justify scrutiny and selective development, not permanent protection for every assembler or component. The right unit of assessment is often the product or process, not the entire sector.
Scale is crucial. Investment in moulds, testing or automated lines must be recovered over sufficient output; short runs make each unit expensive. Too many models fragment demand in a small market, while differing specifications prevent vendors from supplying the same part to several assemblers. Policy should encourage viable specialisation, common components where feasible, supplier consolidation, and access to replacement and export markets. A vendor serving several customers can reach volumes that no single low-volume model offers. Competition policy must accompany consolidation, so that scale raises productivity rather than market power.
Upstream supply matters too. Reliable access to automotive-grade steel, engineering plastics and specialised chemicals affects quality, cost, lead times, and working capital. A competitive local supplier can shorten delivery and support joint development, but domestic steel or petrochemical production alone guarantees neither.
Pakistan need not make every input before it can export. Where domestic production lacks scale or technology, predictable access to competitively priced imports is essential; forcing manufacturers to buy costly local inputs shifts protection upstream and erodes downstream competitiveness. The goal is an efficient supply chain combining viable domestic capabilities with dependable imports, not local-content targets.
Market access is the next missing piece. Cutting Pakistan’s import tariffs does nothing to lower the duties its exporters face abroad. Preferential trade agreements can open larger markets, but their value depends on product coverage, rules of origin, and real commercial opportunities. They should be negotiated around what Pakistan can competitively supply and what investors could realistically produce. 
Buyers also weigh security. Export relationships depend on plant visits, technical assistance, audits, and dependable delivery. Insecurity, transport disruptions or barriers to foreign experts can cancel out a competitive price. Buyers pay for reliability, and investors need confidence that people, equipment and goods can travel safely.
How, then, should protection be withdrawn?
Activities with no credible route to competitiveness should have a clear exit timetable. Those with demonstrable potential should receive temporary support tied to investment, productivity, quality, energy efficiency, and a narrowing price gap with imports. Government should accept published obligations on costs and business conditions. An independent review should distinguish policy failures from outdated equipment, inadequate scale, or poor management. Verified government failures could justify limited adjustments to the tariff timetable, each with a firm expiry. Industry must not gain a permanent veto over reform.
Strategic exceptions should remain narrow. Food security can justify agricultural resilience without self-sufficiency in every crop. Defence can justify selected domestic capabilities despite higher costs, subject to periodic review of their security value and expense.
Lower tariffs on inputs remove one obstacle to exports. They cannot supply scale, modern technology, efficiency, market access, or security. Pakistan needs a reciprocal bargain: industry must earn support through performance, and the government must deliver conditions for competition. Neither should hand consumers an indefinite bill for its failures. 
The writeris a former CEO of Unilever Pakistan and of the Pakistan Business Council.
Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

topic: Industrial Policy and Competitiveness in Pakistan
whyMatters: This article does not directly address Pakistan's role in ECO or regional integration. However, it is highly relevant for understanding the foundational domestic economic reforms—specifically regarding industrial competitiveness, trade policy, and supply chain efficiency—that are prerequisite for Pakistan to effectively engage in any regional or global economic framework, including ECO. summary: Indefinite protection is detrimental to industrial competitiveness, raising costs, blunting innovation, and rewarding inefficiency, ultimately financed by consumers and public expense.

The National Tariff Policy 2025-30 aims to reduce protection and lower input costs, but tariff cuts are insufficient without complementary government actions to reduce state-imposed production costs (e.g., energy, tax refunds, regulation).

A credible industrial strategy requires distinguishing between industries with no competitiveness prospects, those with potential, and a narrow set of strategic capabilities, avoiding indiscriminate support or withdrawal.

Achieving competitiveness depends on factors beyond tariffs, including scale, efficient upstream supply chains (combining local capabilities and reliable imports), market access (through PTAs), and national security.

Protection should be withdrawn with clear timetables, linked to performance (investment, productivity, efficiency), and contingent on government meeting its obligations regarding business conditions, forming a 'reciprocal bargain' with industry.

title: Harvesting rackets
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
ORGAN vending rarely leaves the spotlight. The FIA and the Human Organ Transplantation Authority recently took five suspects into custody for their involvement in unlawful renal transplants at a residential location in Islamabad. The network comprisedagents, a doctor, a nurse, and a laboratory facilitator, among others. Tests were run with fake referrals and false family names. Reportedly, the gang’s transplant scams extended to Peshawar. The Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, enacted to end the abuse of the vulnerable for a hefty profit, is over a decade old. Sadly, the laxity in the criminal justice system not only continues to feed odious rackets of this sort with all the necessary equipment and facilitation, it has also rendered the law ineffective.
Clamping down on organ trade rings involves plugging the loopholes, which include the health authorities’ failure to enforce controls. All chapters of Hota in the country are as much to be blamed as the corrupt medics. The authority’s failure to ensure legalised transplants and screened donors, combined with a lack of vigilance in spotting dubious practices, brings Pakistan close to becoming an organ sale hub once again. Medics found complicit must face lifelong bans, and public and private venues of such crimes should be sealed. The courts, too, should address the issue with as much strictness as the law allows. Advocacy for cadaver organs and legal transplants must be clear and consistent. In the absence of modern databanks and fast-track courts, security personnel will only lurch from one raid to another without taking effective action. To dismantle a global menace, an international partnership plan consisting of security agencies and health officials is crucial. Law enforcers should be aware of the latest protocols to stay ahead of their game. A fragile economy is fertile ground for despair and poverty — the lifeblood of dehumanising practices.
Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026
